This modder thought opening a window was too much work, so he did something cool about it

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

u/Motor_Attention1865 on Reddit didn't like how his PC added extra heat to his room in the winter, so he went the extra mile to dump the heat outside in a fashion similar to mini-split air conditioners. The external cooling system is controlled by an Arduino Mega that the PC communicates with when it needs extra cooling. The system opens a three-way valve to route coolant outside and prevents condensation by keeping the coolant temperature above the dew point.

Our intrepid modder's room has heated floors, and the PC was dumping too much heat under the table where his PC sits, even in 25 °F (-4 °C) weather. He grew tired of manually opening a window to regulate the temperature in his space, so he put in much more effort to create a split cooling system that puts another radiator outside in the below-freezing temperatures, cooling down the PC significantly.

Motor_Attention1865's build itself is impressive enough, with a delidded Core Ultra 7 270K Plus cooled by a Thermal Grizzly 1851 Mycro Pro direct-die water block with Thermal Grizzly Conductonaut Extreme liquid compound. Not only is his RTX 4070 Ti Super also watercooled with a Bykski water block, but the 2x24GB DDR5-8400 G.Skill RAM is also watercooled using Bykski heat spreaders with an IceManCooler two-channel water block. The cooling system within the PC has two radiators: a 120mm in the back and a 360mm in the front, all fed by an EK Kinetic D5 pump-reservoir.

The external cooling system, however, is even more impressive. The 240mm outdoor radiator with two Noctua iPPC-3000 fans isn’t outrageous, but the automated system that makes it useful is what’s interesting. Next to the PC is a box with a Bykski D5 pump and reservoir that pushes water outside, but it doesn’t use the external radiator until the PC needs the extra cooling.

Upon startup, the PC runs a Python script that communicates with an Arduino Mega connected to three temperature probes checking the coolant temperature and three more temperature and humidity sensors that monitor the PC case and the ambient air. The sensors give the Arduino Mega information on where to switch the motorized three-way valve depending on the temperature and humidity.

The problem with extreme cold in any PC is condensation. If coolant gets below the dew point of the environment, condensation forms, potentially shorting out PC components. To prevent this disaster, the Arduino determines the dew point based on the humidity and temperature of the room and in the PC. Motor_Attention1865 set the Arduino to close off the outside radiator at +10 °C above the dew point, or +5 °C during benchmarking, allowing for low temperatures without risking droplets forming in the PC.

Because of the freezing or below-freezing temperatures at which this external loop is meant to operate, Motor_Attention1865 also added pure ethylene glycol to the Aquacomputer Double Protect Ultra Clear coolant in the loop, lowering its freezing point from -18 °C to -28 °C.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Thanks to the supplemental cooling system and delidding, the system achieves temperatures below 50 °C under heavy use. According to Motor_Attention1865, the RTX 4070 Ti sits at 37 °C and the CPU hovers around 45-50 °C while gaming. Temperatures were higher in benchmarks, however — in Cinebench R23, the CPU sat at 52 °C, while in 3DMark Steel Nomad, the GPU was at 48 °C.

Above all, however, Motor_Attention1865 no longer needs to bother himself with opening a window if their room gets too hot with the PC under load. It's the small things.

#10407. This company is giving workers time off to play the new ‘Grand Theft Auto’

With the highly anticipated release of Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI just around the corner, one company is unveiling a new perk for its employees: paid time off for gaming.

In an initiative it’s calling “Logi Game Day,” consumer electronics firm Logitech announced Tuesday that each of its 7,000 workers will receive one paid day off per year to play video games.

Along with hosting a streaming event at its Americas headquarters in San Jose on November 19, the company says it is “formally recognizing the cognitive and professional benefits of gaming.”

“It’s time to retire the stereotype that gaming is a waste of time,” said CEO Hanneke Faber. “As a company designing products for work and play, we see every day how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other.”

It’s no coincidence that Logi Game Day falls on the same day as one of the most-hyped video game releases in recent memory. Grand Theft Auto VI is the first new title in the best-selling series in 13 years, and many workers are already planning on catching “GTA flu” to make the most of release day.  

In one survey of 1,000 U.S. adults who work full-time and regularly play video games, 39% said they planned to request time off in advance to play the game, 36% said they planned to call in sick on release day, and 32% said they would work from home.

The Wall Street Journal has already warned of a “work blackout,” and a Spanish economist has estimated that the release of GTA VI could cost the U.S. $1 billion in lost productivity.

Clearly, Logitech is unbothered by such concerns. The company, which sells gaming equipment through its dedicated gaming brand, Logitech G, has published research showing that gamers believe gaming builds real-world confidence, reduces anxiety, and even corresponds with improved performance at work.

“Play is not the opposite of work,” declared Elaine Laird, Logitech chief people officer. “When people have dedicated time to log off, decompress, and immerse themselves in play, they return with clearer focus, renewed energy, and fresh approaches to complex challenges.”

#10406. United Airlines just made a big change to flight bookings. Here’s why Delta and American aren’t following suit

United Airlines is banning personal AI assistants from booking and modifying tickets on its system, a change that could see other airlines follow suit.

The Chicago-based carrier updated its contract of carriage on Wednesday, prohibiting the use of AI agents to “make, modify or service a ticket, and/or purchase any service or product.”

In its statement, the airline cited concerns that third-party AI assistants can expose passengers’ sensitive information, and that actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases or account changes. United also noted that automated AI actions could potentially violate Federal Aviation Administration or Department of Transportation regulations—noting, for example, that flight check-in requires passengers to acknowledge that their bags don’t contain any banned items.

The carrier may be taking its cue from other industries as it cited that corporate leaders of banks and retail companies have taken similar actions regarding AI agents, stating, “We encourage others to consider measures that preserve the data and security of their customers and strengthen safety.”

As is often the case for the industry, other airlines may follow United’s lead, though none of the other major U.S. carriers have similarly banned AI agents—yet. Just last month, Southwest Airlines announced a plugin partnership with ChatGPT to “offer a simpler, more direct path from inspiration and discovery to booking options” with the airline.

Here’s how the other major carriers are approaching AI tools for booking.

DELTA AND AMERICAN: ‘EVALUATING’ AI

United is one of the three largest carriers serving the U.S., along with Delta Air Lines and American Airlines. Delta and American both indicated to Fast Company that some AI tools have booking privileges on their systems, though they continue to evaluate the landscape.

“Some AI tools are ​able to facilitate the purchase of American Airlines tickets,” a company spokesperson said. “At the same time, protecting our ​customers and their experience remains our priority. We actively monitor traffic across our website ​and app, and ​can investigate, manage, ​or block automated traffic when necessary ​to protect our ​customers and their experience.”

A spokesperson for Delta told Fast Company that if an AI tool can authenticate a passenger’s credentials, then it can complete a booking on their behalf, but noted that even if passengers use AI tools, they’re ultimately responsible for overseeing any actions and authorizing any transactions taken by these assistants on their behalf. 

“We currently support certain interactions with AI assistants when they can be appropriately authenticated, while maintaining additional safeguards for sensitive transactions,” the company said in a statement to Fast Company. “We’re continuing to evaluate how new technology, including external AI agents, could enhance the way customers engage with Delta, always with security and the customer experience in mind.”

Representatives for Southwest, JetBlue, Alaska, and Frontier airlines didn’t immediately respond to Fast Company’s requests for comment.

Shares of United fell 1.8% on Wednesday, while the broader S&P 500 Index rose 1.3%.

#10403. Can anyone really stop the AI data center boom? What could happen next now that voters have spoken

On Election Day, Americans made their opinions about the AI data center boom clear.

Now it’s up to those newly elected legislators to rein in the country’s high-speed data center development. And there’s a lot they can actually do—particularly on the local level.

Data centers were “dealt a resounding blow in the midterm elections,” Mandy DeRoche, director of emerging issues at Earthjustice, said at a press event on November 11. 

Across 10 states, residents overwhelmingly voted for ballot measures to pause development, require public approval for projects, restrict data center electricity use, and link financial assurances to tax incentives. 

Congressional and state-level candidates who promised to address AI data center development also won in large numbers. The total number of governors supporting moratoriums will now represent states with 41% of the country’s planned data center developments, according to Earthjustice. 

How developers fast-tracked data center projects

The data center industry has a history of limiting public information around its projects and a track record of skirting regulations and oversight.

Developers have demanded that government officials sign nondisclosure agreements, denying the public information—and a chance to weigh in.

They’ve also split their projects into smaller permits, sometimes applying for one project’s permits under multiple corporations. That strategy, called “segmentation,” can fast-track approval and conceal the true scope of a project, allowing developers to sidestep more rigorous environmental reviews. 

Still, activists who have been working to protect communities from the harms of data centers are hopeful.

“I’ve never been part of a movement like this before,” said Sarah Friedman, cofounder of Better Data Center Project, an advocacy group that works with communities facing data center development. 

The effort to push back on rampant data center development has “created new alliances, new support, and I think new awareness of Big Tech and the role it plays,” she said. 

It’s also been a bipartisan issue, DeRoche noted, and there’s precedent for action.

“Harmful data center development has been reined in when a state regulator acts, and acts in its community’s interest,” she said. “And I’m optimistic that that will increasingly happen after last week, with new agency heads, with new governors.”

What can actually be done?

So what can the midterm winners actually do about data centers? 

On the state level, lawmakers can ensure that project info is public and accessible by banning NDAs and allowing for community engagement. For projects that are building their own power, lawmakers can require clean energy that meets “new, near, and now standards.”

“That means that they’re building new clean energy resources, not taking existing clean energy resources that would otherwise benefit the grid,” said Callie Rabinovitz, research and policy analyst with the Earthjustice Clean Energy Program. “They must be online when the data center comes online to ensure there’s no fossil fuel bridge power, and they should match the data center’s load 24/7.”

State legislators can require “meaningful” environmental reviews, she added, that look at the cumulative impact of these data centers and their electricity generation. That means considering what pollution already exists in a region, and ensuring that a data center’s base power is not reviewed separately from its backup generators. 

State legislators can repeal tax incentives for data centers that have cost municipalities hundreds of millions of dollars. They can require that data center developers cover decommissioning costs, as well as the costs for any new grid infrastructure that may be needed if an off-grid data center eventually does connect to the grid, “which we expect most of them will,” Rabinovitz said. 

And they can make sure data center moratoriums are actually effective. 

“Not all moratoria are created equal,” DeRoche said.

When outgoing Texas Governor Greg Abbott issued a data center pause, for example, state regulators at the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) still moved forward with 35 permitting actions for data center projects. 

Now Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned on a data center pause, could appoint at least two new commissioners to TCEQ. Voters in the midterms also elected a Democrat to head the Texas Railroad Commission, which regulates the state’s oil and gas industry. 

That commissioner “was not the oil and gas industry’s pick to win the seat,” Commission Shift, a nonprofit watchdog group, told local outlet KERA News. Texas voters also elected a new district attorney who has spoken out against data centers and in support of more local involvement in those projects. 

Much of the permitting decisions for data center projects are made at the state and local level, so those legislators have many opportunities to regulate the industry. Congress can still take action, too. 

In the House and Senate, there’s room to establish guardrails around data center development on public lands, and to require more transparency around energy and water use and overall emissions from these projects. Congress can also pass enforceable ratepayer protections that do not incentivize more gas development and therefore more pollution.

With Democrats controlling both chambers come January, they can establish stronger oversight of the Environmental Protection Agency and other federal departments to ensure they’re protecting communities from harmful environmental impacts with laws that are already on the books.

Because so much of the permitting happens at the local level, Congress can also make sure that local rights to regulate are protected. 

Changes in legislation could allow the entire data center conversation to be reframed, according to Meg Slattery, staff scientist at Earthjustice.

“We are hoping that this creates an opportunity to refocus on addressing the climate crisis and building a just clean energy transition,” she said, “rather than orienting the government towards accommodating a hyperscale data center buildout at any cost.”

#10399. Jensen Huang may be out at Nvidia: The rise and fall of a key figure in the AI boom

Jensen Huang has, for more than three decades, been the driving force behind Nvidia, transforming a video game graphic chipmaker into one of the most impactful companies of the AI era. Now, in a remarkable turn of events, the 63-year-old CEO may be on his way out.

The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang, following allegations of a second extramarital affair, this one with a company executive who reports to him. That bombshell came just days after reports emerged of a liaison with a woman who led Singaporean data center firm Megaspeed who is also suspected of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia’s board launched an investigation after Huang acknowledged that affair, but said it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised.

The revelation of a second affair, however, this time involving a subordinate (reportedly Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare), reinforces concerns about Huang’s judgment—and perhaps alters the company’s potential legal exposure. The board was set to meet as early as today to determine his future, according to The Journal, as a scandal initially centered on national security grows into a broader crisis of corporate governance.

Should Huang indeed be given the boot, he’ll leave behind a company that helped transform modern computing—and one built to an extraordinary degree around him.

From gaming chips to AI dominance

In 1993, following stints at AMD and chipmaker LSI Logic, Huang cofounded Nvidia with engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. Their bet—that increasingly sophisticated computer graphics would require specialized processors—proved to be prescient. Six years after launch, Nvidia introduced its GeForce 256, marketed as the world’s first graphics processing unit, or GPU. By handling complex visual calculations far more efficiently than general-purpose processors, GPUs basically kicked gaming into hyperdrive.

Arguably Huang’s most consequential bet came in 2006, when Nvidia introduced CUDA, a software platform that lets programmers harness GPUs for tasks beyond graphics. It was an expensive and long-term investment: Huang was banking on the idea that GPUs’ ability to perform thousands of calculations simultaneously could open up entirely new markets for Nvidia beyond video games. And boy, was he right. 

In 2012, researchers used Nvidia GPUs to train AlexNet, a breakthrough neural network that helped usher in the modern era of deep learning. A decade later, the release of ChatGPT sent demand for Nvidia’s chips soaring as Silicon Valley raced to build increasingly powerful AI systems. Nvidia was ready, offering not just advanced chips but an entire software ecosystem built around them. “We are at the iPhone moment of AI,” Huang declared in March 2023.

The results of Huang’s wager have been jaw-dropping. Nvidia’s chips have become essential infrastructure for companies like Microsoft and Google, as well as a number of leading AI labs. In its most recent quarterly earnings report, Nvidia reported $96.2 billion in revenue—more than double the previous year’s figure. (Of that, a staggering $89 billion came from its data center business alone.)

All the while, Huang retained an extraordinary degree of control over the company, involving himself in the minutiae of chip development and famously eschewing one-on-one meetings in favor of group discussions. He also became something of a rock star in the tech world—one who was instantly recognizable on account of his beloved leather jacket.

The risk of building a company around one person

According to Fortune, Huang has approximately 60 direct reports, an unusually flat management structure, and no chief operating officer. Nvidia has also never publicly identified a successor, leaving no obvious heir to the multitrillion-dollar company. (Huang, for his part, has apparently said he doesn’t believe in succession planning.)

That arrangement may have helped facilitate a streamlined operation—and it netted the company a lot of money. But now, in light of Huang’s potential removal, it also exposes the risks of building a company around a single individual.

Ironically, it could be the second affair that ultimately seals Huang’s fate, even though the first would seem to carry far greater consequences. His alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset—an executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer that was previously investigated by the U.S. Commerce Department over possible chip diversions to China—has already attracted the attention of lawmakers, many of whom question whether sensitive information could have been compromised.

“This is not just personal foibles,” a senior government official who focuses on AI told Fast Company earlier this week. 

Sure enough, three House committee chairs have requested a closed-door meeting with Huang, who also now faces a proposed shareholder class action over the scandal. The alleged affair with a subordinate, meanwhile, raises a different set of concerns, and could open up new lanes of potential legal exposure for Nvidia.

The timing is particularly precarious. Nvidia shares fell roughly 8% in after-hours trading Wednesday following the reports, and uncertainty over its leadership could reverberate well beyond the company’s stock price. And it just so happens that Anthropic is reportedly preparing to go public as soon as next week, amid growing investor anxiety over the enormous sums being poured into AI. 

For 33 years Nvidia’s fortunes have been inseparable from Huang’s. Now, at a moment when much of the tech industry’s fortunes are tied to Nvidia, the company may have to prove it can thrive without him.

#10396. Why PTO in the U.S. is so unbelievably bad

Most countries around the world offer workers some form of paid time off (PTO). So, how did the U.S. become one of the few outliers that has no federally guaranteed paid vacation, maternity, family, or bereavement leave—let alone sick time? 

The factors are many, ranging from cultural expectations to legal ones. In America, PTO is up to the employer or local officials, rather than treated as something every working person deserves.

“I think that has shaped how we view time off,” says Cory McCruden, CEO of Best Upon Request, a concierge service focused on employee well-being. “It can feel like a benefit your employer gives you rather than a normal part of working and living.”

PTO is certainly a privilege for workers in the U.S. That reality makes life harder for everyone, from the parent who needs to leave work early to pick up a child to the individual who woke up with the flu. Thanksgiving’s just around the corner, and while it’s a federal holiday, many workers may feel anxious about asking for extra time off. A single day is hardly generous, especially when traveling to see family can be so time-consuming.

The current situation comes in spite of the fact that taking PTO has been proven to improve employee retention—increasing with the number of days off—and offer psychological benefits to the individual. 

So, why is the state of PTO in America so bad? Things have gone wrong to get to this point, but there could be ways to turn it around. 

How many employees in the U.S. get PTO?

Again, PTO is not nationally guaranteed in any form. 

According to the Center for Economic and Policy Research, about 23% of the U.S. civilian workforce gets no paid vacation days. This number jumps to 43% when looking at the 10% lowest-paid workers. For employees who do receive paid vacation time, the average number of days given is just 10. In comparison, the think tank reports that 25 of the 38 member countries of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) guarantee at least 20 vacation days. 

The numbers are similar for sick leave, with the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reporting that 17% of U.S. workers don’t have access to paid sick leave in 2026.

These figures don’t take into account the fact that some employers even ban taking unpaid leave. 

In the U.S., the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) allows certain employees the right to take 12 weeks of unpaid family or medical leave for reasons such as childbirth. Meanwhile, OECD countries—even with zero weeks from the U.S. factored in—offer an average of 18.4 weeks paid maternity leave. 

The U.S. joins Papua New Guinea in the tiny list of countries offering none. 

Employers who provide paid time off might specify a number of days for each type of leave. However, it can often be given as one chunk of time covering all forms—leading to potential problems. 

“An issue with this approach is that workers may not use the time when they really need it, either because it is gone or because they must hoard it for another hardship,” says Candice Vander Weerdt, a PTO researcher and senior college lecturer in the business department at Cleveland State University. “Perhaps they used the last of their PTO during a family vacation and now cannot take time off when they catch the flu.”

PTO laws in the U.S.

Most places in the U.S. offer PTO solely at the employer’s discretion. However, some states have taken it upon themselves to protect this right by law. According to the U.S. Department of Labor, 18 states and Washington, D.C., require private employers to offer paid sick leave if an employee or a family member is unwell. 

Thirteen states, Washington D.C., and Puerto Rico have laws requiring paid family and medical leave. 

At the same time, half of all states have some form of a preemptive law, meaning they prohibit local officials from passing laws requiring PTO, the Economic Policy Institute reports. In some cases, these laws prevent local governments from passing ordinances that differ from state rules. However, most of them ban any form of mandated sick or family leave policies.

As McCruden puts it: “Your experience in the U.S. can depend a lot on where you work and where you live.” 

Having PTO isn’t enough—the culture needs to change

Even if workers do have PTO, it doesn’t mean they’re going to take it. 

“I think we need to talk less about how much PTO people have and more about whether they actually feel comfortable using it,” McCruden says. “A company can offer plenty of time off, but if people don’t feel like they can use it, the benefit only goes so far.” 

Workers might be reluctant to take their PTO for fear of retaliation or falling behind, says Molly Weston Williamson, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress who’s researching PTO. In a 2023 Pew Research study, 46% of employees reported not taking all of their paid time off. Some of the most common reasons were worrying about falling behind (49%) and feeling bad about coworkers having extra work (43%). Weston Williamson points to structural issues around insufficient staffing and employee capability as fueling these factors. 

Participants also cited very harmful repercussions, with 19% thinking it will hurt their chances of advancement and 16% thinking they might lose their job. Another 12% of people reported being discouraged by their boss from taking time off. 

“We have an environment in which even workers who, on paper, have access to some kind of paid time off, don’t feel secure in taking it,” Weston Williamson says. “And then that’s particularly true for workers who are newer to their employer or for Black workers.” 

Managers, salaried workers, and higher earners were also less likely to use all of their PTO. 

According to Weston Williamson, the lack of laws mandating PTO can contribute to these issues. She explains that when PTO is required by law, it typically protects the ability of workers to take leave without facing repercussions or having requests turned down simply because the timing is inconvenient for others.

McCruden points to another potential reason: “In America, we tend to associate being busy and available with being committed to our jobs. Other countries have made paid time away from work a more standard part of working life.”

How to change the state of PTO in the U.S.

Both individuals and companies can work to change PTO access and the culture around it. You can take steps to improve things for yourself and others. Vander Weerdt recommends negotiating the amount of PTO you get before accepting a job offer or a promotion. 

“Some managers may not realize how important the benefit is to their employees,” she says. “Speaking up and sharing the real benefits of paid time off can be rather meaningful.”

If you’re a manager, then you’re in a position to grant PTO requests and normalize taking it by setting an example. 

You can also take steps outside of the office. “Individuals can work to create change through advocacy for public policies that guarantee paid leave at the local, state, and federal level, as well as advocating for robust, well-designed, and culturally supported paid leave policies within their employers,” Weston Williamson says.  

On the company side, there are so many things that can be done to improve PTO for employees. Much of it comes down to encouragement and modeling behavior. “Create the policy and then make the policy real,” Weston Williamson adds. “Make sure that people have a realistic ability to reliably actually take that time, and that when they do so, they are secure in doing so.” 

McCruden explains that leaders set an example by taking time off, determining coverage for while they’re away, and disconnecting while gone. This precedent allows the rest of the team, or even the company, to do the same. 

“It has to be made clear that our position is, ‘We want everyone to use all of their leave,’” Weston Williamson says. “We think that’s an actively good thing that we are here to support and encourage, and that we want leadership all the way through to be with that message.”

#10394. How Motion Design Improves SaaS Onboarding and Feature Adoption

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most SaaS products don't lose users because the software is bad. They lose users in the first few minutes, before anyone has seen what the product can actually do. Someone signs up, lands on an empty dashboard, feels a flicker of confusion, and quietly leaves. The industry has a name for the gap between signing up and getting value: activation. Closing it is one of the hardest problems in product design.

Motion design is one of the most underused tools for closing that gap. Used well, animation isn't decoration sprinkled on at the end. It's a layer of communication that tells users where to look, confirms that their actions worked, and makes a complex interface feel learnable instead of overwhelming. This article looks at why motion influences behaviour during onboarding, the specific patterns that move the needle on activation and feature adoption, and how to build them responsibly as a developer — with an eye on performance and accessibility throughout.

Motion works in onboarding because it speaks to how human perception actually operates, not because it looks modern. A few principles do most of the heavy lifting.

It directs attention. The eye is drawn to movement before it reads a single word. A gently pulsing button or an element that slides into view tells a new user where to go next without a paragraph of instructions. On a crowded first-run screen, that guidance is the difference between a confident first action and a confused exit.

It preserves context. When a panel expands, a card flips, or a new view slides in from the right, a short transition shows users where things came from and where they went. This spatial continuity keeps people oriented. Interfaces that snap instantly between states force the user to re-scan the screen each time and silently rebuild their mental model.

It confirms actions. Every click, toggle, and form submission is a small question: did that work? A quick visual response — a checkmark drawing itself, a row settling into place — answers it immediately. Without that feedback, users repeat actions, doubt the system, or assume something broke.

It shapes perceived performance. A thoughtful loading animation or skeleton screen makes a wait feel shorter and the product feel responsive, even when the underlying request takes exactly as long. Perception of speed is part of the experience, and motion is how you manage it.

These are the patterns that reliably help new users reach their first win.

Onboarding doesn't end after the first session. Most SaaS products keep shipping features, and each one faces its own adoption problem: users settle into a few familiar workflows and never discover the rest. Motion is how you reintroduce the product to people who already think they know it.

Contextual nudges that appear in motion — a tooltip that eases in near a newly relevant button, a gentle highlight on a feature the moment a user hits the limit it solves — are far more effective than a generic email. They arrive at the point of need and use movement to pull attention without hijacking the screen.

"What's new" reveals can announce an update with a small, well-timed animation rather than a modal that gets dismissed on reflex. A badge that animates in, or a panel that slides open on the first visit to a page, respects the user's flow while still being noticed.

Animated demonstrations carry the most weight for genuinely complex features. Showing a feature in motion — rather than describing it in text — lets users grasp a multi-step workflow in seconds. For intricate capabilities, this is where a short, purpose-made explainer earns its place, a point we return to in the next section.

The right tool depends on how complex the animation is and where it lives. Roughly in order of weight:

CSS transitions and keyframe animations should be your default. They cover the large majority of onboarding motion — hovers, state changes, highlights, progress bars — and the browser can run them efficiently. Reach for JavaScript only when CSS genuinely can't express what you need.

The Web Animations API gives you CSS-level performance with programmatic control, which matters when animations depend on data or user input, or need to be sequenced and interrupted. SitePoint's guide to the Web Animations API is a solid introduction, and the broader web animation archive covers libraries like GSAP for orchestrating complex timelines.

Lottie is the bridge between designer-made animation and the web. Designers export vector animations as JSON, and a lightweight player renders them natively at small file sizes — ideal for polished illustrative moments like success states and animated empty states, without hand-coding every frame.

Pre-rendered video is the right call when a feature is genuinely involved and a looping CSS animation or a tooltip simply can't carry the explanation. A short, well-produced walkthrough can compress a multi-step workflow into something a user absorbs in under a minute, which is why many teams lean on a dedicated SaaS explainer video for their most complex features and onboarding moments. The trade-off is weight and production effort, so reserve video for the handful of places where it genuinely outperforms in-interface motion, lazy-load it, and never autoplay it with sound.

Motion that stutters does more damage than no motion at all, and motion that ignores accessibility can actively harm users. Two disciplines keep animation on the right side of that line.

For performance, animate the properties the browser can handle cheaply: transform and opacity. These can run on the compositor thread without triggering layout or paint, which is what lets animation hold a smooth 60fps. Animating properties like width, height, top, or left forces the browser to recalculate layout on every frame and is the usual cause of janky motion. Keep animations short — most interface transitions should land between 150 and 300 milliseconds — because motion that overstays its welcome makes a product feel slow.

For accessibility, honour the prefers-reduced-motion media query. Some users experience dizziness, nausea, or disorientation from movement, and the operating system lets them ask for less of it. Respecting that setting is straightforward:

Beyond that, never let an animation block interaction. If a user has to wait for a flourish to finish before they can click, the motion is working against them. Animation should support the task and then get out of the way.

Motion design is a product decision, so treat it like one and measure it. The metrics that matter map directly to the problems motion is meant to solve.

Treat animations as hypotheses and A/B test them. Ship the animated onboarding step to half of your new users and measure activation against the control. Motion should earn its place with data, not assumptions — and occasionally the data will tell you an animation is slowing people down, which is just as useful to know.

The best onboarding motion is the kind users never consciously notice. It simply makes the product feel clear, responsive, and easy to learn — guiding attention, confirming actions, and turning a complex interface into something approachable. That's the real payoff: not animation for its own sake, but fewer confused users, faster time to value, and features that actually get discovered.

Start small. Pick the single point in your onboarding where users most often stall, add one purposeful animation that removes the confusion, and measure what happens. Motion, used deliberately, is one of the most direct levers you have on activation and adoption — and like any good tool, it works best when it draws no attention to itself.

The data center boom is negatively affecting Ukraine's war effort.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine sparked a new era of drone warfare. Russian invaders first used drones with fiber-optic tethers to combat electronic warfare on the front lines, but both sides now use these jam-proof drones. Against that backdrop, the AI data center buildout is making it harder for Ukraine to buy the fiber-optic spools that it needs to continue scaling its drone manufacturing capabilities. A research and development representative for BlueBird Tech, a Ukrainian defense firm specializing in drones, told Ars Technica in an interview that prices of fiber optic cables have risen around six to 10 times in the past couple of years as AI data center demand soaks up more and more of the supply of this resource.

According to that interview, It’s estimated that Ukraine and Russia are producing around 50,000 fiber optic drones monthly, with each drone capable of ranges of up to 62 miles. But Ukraine has only been able to acquire 72 miles of fiber optic cable from Chinese suppliers during August 2025, whereas Russia imported a whopping 328,000 miles during that same month. It was estimated that Russia acquired 37 million miles of fiber during the entirety of 2025, accounting for over 10% of the global production.

What makes matters worse for Ukrainian defenders is that there is an estimated 111-million-mile shortfall in fiber optic cable supply across the world, adding to the various shortages that the data center industry has faced in recent years. Aside from the material shortfall, Ukraine faces trade barriers in acquiring more fiber. The BlueBird representative claimed that some Chinese companies have outright refused to sell Ukraine fiber optic cables.

China is the primary supplier of this material, so it’s easier for Russia to obtain them through its massive land border with the country. While Ukraine could purchase fiber optic cables from suppliers located in other countries, that's not much of an alternative. The BlueBird rep notes: "there can be intermediaries in other countries, and prices can differ depending on the country and the purchasing route. But in the end, China remains the main source of the fiber optic material we are talking about.”

There has also been talk of producing fiber optic cables domestically in Ukraine, but such manufacturing requires specially trained personnel who must practice on the already limited supply of fiber optic cables. Even if manufacturers automate production, they still require experienced personnel who can oversee the line and ensure the quality of the final product.

The data center build out has been causing all kinds of shortages. We’ve seen supply shortfalls in GPUs, memory chips, and even PCBs, but there’s also shortages in other seemingly unrelated industries like power infrastructure, optical transceivers, and even in critical skilled labor like electricians. This overwhelming demand has started affecting other industries not related to computing, like cars, home construction, and now, fiber optic attack drones.

#10390. What it’s like to change careers when you’re at the top of your game

When Kim Foster was 17, she decided she was going to become a doctor. 

It was a feat that no one in her family had accomplished. “I just strapped in and did what I needed to do to execute on that big goal,” she says. Foster worked toward getting into medical school, graduating, and all the subsequent training. Then she practiced medicine for 20 years. “It was great for a while,” she says, “until it wasn’t anymore.” 

During the last few years as a family doctor, Foster noticed a pattern. She was often seeing patients when they were already experiencing problems—diabetes, chronic pain, heart disease. By the time they got in front of her, she says, “things were starting to fall apart.” 

She began to feel a pull toward helping people make different decisions, and also yearned to do something creative. Eventually, she decided to walk away from her medical career. Now the 54-year-old helps those who are looking to make pivots or reinvent themselves in their lives through her YouTube channel and online courses. 

Outgrowing your established career later in life

Like Foster, Alexandra Aileru knows what it’s like to outgrow one’s career. The 35-year-old had worked in the education sector for eight years. She’d already been thinking about leaving her field for a while. Then she became pregnant and realized she needed to make an exit. 

Aileru transitioned into project management before realizing a few years in that she’d hit what she calls the peak of what she wanted to achieve in that role. At the end of 2023, she started posting on TikTok about her career pivot experience. She got a lot of questions from her audience and recognized that there was a market to help people with similar transformations. In 2024, she went all in on her business, Confident Career Switch. The company’s motto, she says, is to help people “get unstuck with their careers.”  

Aileru and Foster might have made pivots during different stages of their lives, but both transitioned when they were more established and had responsibilities. Like Aileru, Foster had children to take care of. She was the main breadwinner in her family, so transitioning away from medicine required building what she calls an off-ramp. 

For Foster, that meant operating in a half-in, half-out capacity. She reduced her hours as a doctor while building her income from various side projects. When she finally left medicine for good, she’d already made more money from her other projects than she had as a practicing physician. 

Wrestling with an identity change and being a beginner 

Practical considerations weren’t the only barriers Foster faced when it came to leaving medicine. She also had to wrestle with a change in identity—something that Aileru says is common among those who want to pivot their careers when they’re already established.

As a doctor, “I was very comfortable with being competent,” Foster says. “People came to me all day long, specifically to ask for my expertise. That was a big part of how I saw myself in the world, and I got a lot of satisfaction out of that.” 

Starting an online business required Foster to be a beginner in something that doesn’t have the same prestige. A lot of those things, like making YouTube videos, “also needed to happen in public,” she says.

Then there was the marketing and drumming up business, something Foster never had to worry about in her career as a physician. Practicing medicine comes with set pathways, an ecosystem, and mentors, she says. The same doesn’t exist in entrepreneurship, where she had to figure out her own next steps, as well as search for people who could help her with various aspects of her business.  

Foster also had to contend with the opinions of other people in her life, many of whom didn’t understand her decision. They wanted to know why she would throw away something she’d spent so long building. 

Two things that helped Foster were working with a coach and enrolling in a coaching training program with others who were also building online businesses. Being exposed to different possibilities, Foster says, helped her realize that we don’t need to get locked into “one way of viewing ourselves.”  

Leveraging your previous experience for the next role

As Foster transitioned into her new venture, she realized just how beneficial her previous experience was. As a primary care physician, she spoke to people every single day, and could also see the value of incorporating her medical experience in her coaching practice. Eventually, that led to a mindset shift where she says she began to see medicine as a “foundation, but not a cage.”

This mindset is something that Aileru sees many people struggle with when they switch careers, particularly those who are established. Because their background isn’t considered linear or traditional in their new careers, they see it as a hindrance, when Aileru says it can be a superpower. After all, she says, “You have a new lens and insights that other people don’t have.” 

At Confident Career Switch, Aileru guides people through a multistage framework to help them get clarity about the transition. She begins by encouraging clients to dig deep into their identity before they start thinking about their skill sets and strengths. 

Next, she urges them to consider their value. For this step, she instructs people to think broadly beyond what they’ve done in the office.

“This could be within an organization, a side hustle that you have, things you’ve done for friends and family,” she says. What you want to identify, she says, “is a repeated skill that keeps showing up.” Maybe you’re naturally great at organizing things, she says, which places you well to work in events. Or maybe you’re great at dealing with difficult stakeholders, which makes you a natural fit for leadership roles, she continues. 

The importance of experimentation

Both Aileru and Foster acknowledge that changing careers at an established stage in your life comes with a set of considerations that may not apply to those who are earlier in their careers. That’s why Foster encourages a period of experimentation prior to making any major transition.

Not everyone knows what their path forward might look like, she says. However, being willing to experiment and explore different interests can reveal pathways or market opportunities. One piece of advice she often shares with clients is to “give themselves permission to question anything that they don’t currently believe about themselves and just say, ‘Well, what if I could learn this? What if I could actually acquire the skills to do that? What would that look like?’”

Foster says that for people who come from established careers with a delineated path, it can be difficult to embrace this period of uncertainty. But she urges them to try and be comfortable with not knowing what’s next, advising, “If you just jump into something that seems like a good idea and it’s got this clear path, you haven’t really given yourself an opportunity to experiment and play with it.” 

When you do that, Foster says, there’s a risk that “you might just end up in the same situation again, where you’ve chosen something that really isn’t a great fit.”

#10389. Want to drive AI innovation? Talk about feelings

The 2026 midterms made one thing clear: Voters are “mad at” AI, as political strategist Rob Flaherty put it.

On the podcast Machine Gods, Flaherty notes that “the story people are saying to themselves is, ‘This thing is in my backyard. It is being used to train stuff that’s gonna take my job away, and I get no say over any of this, and I’m really mad about that.’” An NBC exit poll found that 56% of voters said that AI and data centers were a “crucial or major factor” in their vote for Congress.

It’s obvious that people hate data centers. But workers resent AI rollouts in their workplaces, too. Data tracked on Blood in the Machine shows office worker sentiment toward AI dropped from 81% positive in 2019 to just 43% positive (with 53% negative) by 2026, listing “force-fed tools” as a major grievance. A Gallup global study reported that 74% of Americans are worried about AI, driven by widespread anxiety over job obsolescence and automated layoffs.

These voters are American employees, many of whom are being asked by their employers to “transform” their work lives with AI. You might be thinking: How can someone who voted against fast-moving AI on Tuesday be open and willing to experiment with AI at scale in their work lives? The answer is they can’t. We have a negative bias towards uncertainty, and our AI future is the ultimate uncertainty. Nobody knows what’s going to happen. And as we saw in the election, voters said, “Slow down.”

American employers need to deal with this fact. That doesn’t mean voters—or employees—hate AI. For most of us, AI offers a fundamental paradox: There’s a lot we like about generative AI, how it helps our daily lives. And we are fearful of it. We have to hold that duality.

This matters deeply to any manager or leader who wants their company to adopt AI at scale. When people are fearful and conflicted, they want to find safety. This means we resist change, or we act out against it. “An April 2026 survey of 2,400 knowledge workers across the U.S., U.K., and Europe—including 1,200 C-suite executives—conducted by Writer and Workplace Intelligence found that 29% of employees admitted to actively sabotaging their company’s AI strategy, a figure that jumps to 44% among Gen Z workers,” writes Fortune. It’s very hard to be open, innovative, and experimental when you fear for your future.

Nothing about the election results says stop AI entirely. It says, “Pause and let’s please talk about this.” This has to happen at work, too. In this article, I share how to get started, with two key questions.

Why can’t people change?

I spent decades as a political and advocacy consultant, and clients always asked me the same thing: Why won’t people change their behavior? Why don’t they vote for the candidates who support their interests? Why don’t they exercise? Why won’t they support a policy that will save them money and improve their health? Here’s what I learned, and science backs me up: You can’t change behavior when people are stuck. So why do people get stuck?

  • Change feels dangerous, and it’s safer to stay where you are.
  • We’ve built an “immunity to change.”

In Robert Kegan and Lisa Lahey’s Immunity to Change framework, the idea is that when we can’t make a change we genuinely want, it’s usually not a willpower problem. It’s because some part of us is committed—quietly, even unconsciously—to the opposite. Kegan calls this a psychological immune system. It has one foot on the gas and one on the brake.

When change feels unsafe, our brain, nervous system and body will conspire to keep us in the status quo. After all, its job is to keep us safe. Often, our psychological immune system is run by anxiety. Anxiety is a response to threats we anticipate.

Change with AI came too fast, too soon, too much, which creates a threat response in humans. We freeze, fight, or flee. In his new book, Our Existential Advantage, Enrique Rubio argues that every major technological revolution teaches the same lesson: Things change. Historically, though, the change came slowly enough for society to adjust. The printing press spread knowledge across Europe and helped spark the Renaissance and the Enlightenment, but that took decades. AI is just as transformative, and it’s happening almost overnight. Because the change is so fast, the structures built on the old technology can’t keep up, and nor can we. As a result, many people despair that AI is something that’s happening to us, that it’s inevitable and we don’t have any agency over it.

We feel anxious about AI for very good reason. It threatens our safety, our livelihoods, our children’s futures, our values, and the meaning that we find in work. I’ve heard from employees who resent AI for siphoning off creativity and expertise, or think that it encourages sloppiness or laziness. We work for many different reasons. Although money is important, humans highly value agency at work, and we need meaning and purpose. When we give decisions to AI, what happens to core values like self-reliance, learning, or usefulness? The scholar Ziyaad Bhorat proffers three important abilities that individuals and communities have already identified as worth protecting from AI: work, knowledge and understanding, and decision-making. He writes that work is worth protecting, as is the right to keep our skills from atrophying and from being substituted by machines.

On Election Day, voters took back agency over AI. Their employers need to listen, and it starts with having a different kind of conversation about AI and work.

How to have the right AI conversations

Recently I was a guest on Changing Conversations, a podcast hosted by Katherine Cotter and Stig Albertsen, who lead organizational transformation work at the consultancy Implement. We discussed the opportunity leaders have right now to start conversations with their teams that understand the fundamental paradox of AI, and offer space and time to explore it. These conversations don’t need to have clear next steps and a defined outcome; they simply need to happen.

We are having technical conversations about AI: the opportunity, where to focus, how to roll out transformation and increase proficiency. There’s a real sense of FOMO with AI, a real sense of you’ve got to get with the program. A lot of people feel like admitting any sense of hesitancy or fear might make them weak. They worry that asking questions about AI rollouts might cause them to be viewed as un-innovative, which is ironic, because when you’re feeling stuck, you’re not as innovative. So the key is to get unstuck, and that means digging into our emotions around what AI means to us.

AI brings up a lot of emotions, and most of us are uncomfortable with emotions at work. That’s why this stuff is so important: When you don’t feel your emotions, you can’t make the best decisions. I want people to make good decisions. So I want them to sit for a minute and have this conversation, because when we’re able to name difficult emotions, understand them, and move through, we are able to create change, innovation, and great new things. The threat diminishes and we see a way forward. We regain our agency.

And it can start by asking two simple questions: “When I think of my craft, what makes me feel proud, fulfilled, purposeful?” and then “Does the implementation of AI change anything about this?”

I like to ask people to think of the parts of their craft and work that they really love to do, and that they feel mastery over. For most people, this is a good feeling. When we think about our craft, we feel proud, and we feel a tremendous sense of agency because we have worked hard to master something valuable. And when we then unpack how AI relates to our craft, it can bring up a lot of questions. It can remind us where AI is aligned with our values, and where it’s not. It can make us think about whether AI threatens our craft, or can enhance it, or both. This conversation opens up room to explore more deeply the question of what our AI future means for us.

I think AI gives us an opportunity to face what many of us see as an existential threat and to move through that. That’s how we gain control. Stig noted, “AI…holds an invitation to figure out what is the uniqueness of being human, or even what is my unique gift…. Part of what I do can be handled by other means and supporting tools and technology, and that’s an invitation for me to figure out: What is it that cannot be distributed to someone else, because only I can do that with that specific flavor?”

Questions to ask yourself and your team

I asked Stig: After all the years you’ve been doing this work, what’s the piece of your craft you love most, the thing you’re really good at? Try that yourself, and see what comes up. Sit with it; don’t rush to solve it!

Here are some more helpful questions to ask yourself and your team:

  • What do I love about AI? What has surprised me?
  • What parts of my job do I dislike and wish AI would take?
  • What parts do I love and never want AI to touch? Why do they matter so much?
  • What scares me about AI?
  • What values are underneath all of that?

A few things I’ve learned from running these conversations: The leader goes first, and admits their own messiness. Expect the first few minutes to feel weird; people often look at me blankly until we get to their values or their kids, and then it clicks. Don’t attach a productivity goal. And make room for both/and, as the scholar Wendy Smith would put it. The most common thing I hear is some version of: I love it, it helps me so much, and I’m really worried about my kids.

People are relieved to learn they’re not the only ones holding both. The conversation is the most important part. There are no right or wrong answers, only the beginning of getting unstuck and moving through change.

#10385. What I let AI touch in my solo business—and what stays off-limits

A lot of AI advice suggests that you hand over work to a personal agent, like letting it triage your inbox or shop for you. That’s certainly appealing, since we’re all relentlessly busy and constantly fighting small tasks that take up our time. 

But every time you connect an AI tool to one of your accounts, you’re also answering a second question: What is this tool allowed to do on my behalf? 

For a lot of solopreneurs, that question gets answered by default. You click “allow” on the permissions screen, and the tool can now reach everything in that account. 

I use AI a lot in my business, but I’ve also drawn some very clear boundaries around what it can access.

Sort your tools by what AI can do in them

Every AI tool I use falls into one of three buckets.

Read but not edit. AI can pull information from the tool, but it can’t change anything. This works well for reference material you want AI to draw from without any risk of it being rewritten.

One example, for me, is pulling financial data from QuickBooks. I let Claude analyze some numbers every month, but I don’t want AI making changes to my transactions.

Full editing. AI can create and change things directly in these tools. This makes sense where a mistake is easy to spot and quick to undo.

I use Canva to plan a lot of my marketing material. Nothing is mission-critical, and the full ability to make changes gives me a lot of capabilities to use Claude with Canva.

Off-limits. AI can’t access the tool at all. 

One thing I don’t let AI touch at all is my bank accounts. JP Morgan Chase reported that people were handing over their banking credentials to AI agents like Muse. That’s outside of my comfort zone. 

Workarounds can ease your comfort with AI access 

Some of my most useful setups give AI partial access to a tool. 

Secondary accounts. You might give AI its own limited version of a tool and keep it out of your main account.

I do this with email. I have a secondary email inbox for inbound inquiries to my website. AI can sort and draft replies without touching my main inbox.

Limited permissions

Some tools will let you scope AI to certain projects. I use a database tool called Airtable to manage information for my solo business. Claude can only access certain parts of Airtable, so it can’t inadvertently cause an issue in a tool that I rely on heavily. 

“Supervised” tasks. AI does the work, and nothing moves forward until I approve it. With my email example, Claude can draft a reply to an email but can’t send it. The draft waits for me to review it.

Revisit the boundaries as the tools change

Your boundaries may change over time. AI tools keep adding new connections and capabilities. These changes may make you more or less comfortable with what they can do.

Or you might need to “use AI to fight AI.” I was resistant to letting AI access my email inbox, but the inbound inquiries I get from other people using AI themselves forced me to think differently. My solution was the separate email inbox. 

In the end, I can use AI as much as I do because I decided up front what it can access.

#10384. Samsung bets that you’ll either buy a Galaxy S27 Pro or Ultra next year

Samsung is teeing up to kick off 2027 with an all-new lineup of flagship smartphones, and despite rising prices at your local Best Buy, the brand is still hedging that you’re going to pony up for the most premium model available.

As reported by ETNews, Samsung is currently allotting over 70 percent of its total production capabilities to just the Galaxy S27 Ultra and the new Galaxy S27 “Pro” model expected to launch alongside it. That leaves the plain Galaxy S27 and the larger S27+ on the outside looking in. In comparison to this year’s launch, the Galaxy S26 Ultra made up about 50 percent of this series’ production volume, for a grand total of 18 million units.

Historical performance implies Samsung is probably correct here. While big displays are typically what consumers are drawn to, it does appear that the S27 Pro won’t be all that much smaller than the S27+. Considering the Pro should slot in right around the typical price point as the Plus model, it’s not hard to imagine plenty of would-be S27+ buyers moving to the Pro.

For what it’s worth, Samsung betting big on high-end devices usually pays off. We’re on year two of the Fold series seeing big successes — first with the redesigned Fold 7 in 2025, then with the reshaped Fold 8 this year — and the Galaxy S26 Ultra managed to become the best-selling Android phone in Q2 of this year in a list typically populated by iPhones and cheap Galaxy A-series models. Even with prices constantly on the rise, the people yearn for flagship smartphones. You just have to wonder where that ceiling actually is.

Starbase, Texas, which hosts SpaceX’s Starship rocket program, has just posted a notice of a public hearing for a gas-fired power plant and supercomputing facility within the corporate limits of the city. The project has an initial cost of $24 billion and will apparently be owned by SpaceX. Bloomberg reports that the project could face resistance from incoming Texas governor Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned against approving new data centers until the state's legislature has enacted stronger protections against potential harms from those projects.

Until now, Elon Musk's SpaceXSI has been building out its Colossus I and Colossus II data centers near the Mississippi-Tennessee border, but those projects have faced backlash, attracting a lawsuit from area residents that aims to curb the pollutants produced by the large number of gas turbines required to power those facilities.

Now, it seems that SpaceXSI wants to build another site in Texas that would lie in a city that mostly sits on land owned by SpaceX and whose population mostly comprises its own employees. The project might face reduced local opposition compared to the company's Memphis facilities, as Starbase is essentially a company town for SpaceX. But Hinojosa's arrival in the governor's office could trump that seemingly permissible local regulatory climate.

The project would seem to be a part of SpaceX’s push to build 10 gigawatts of compute in 2027 alone, and the $24 billion budget for this new facility could make it one of the biggest and most expensive data center projects focused on a single site. The company's announcement also notes that the $24 billion outlay it foresees was only for the “initial phases of the projects” and that it could “include future expansions.” That suggests that SpaceXSI could invest in more capacity in Starbase, Texas, going forward, assuming the favorable regulatory climate the company likely hoped for in the area holds.

Beyond its new terrestrial ambitions in Starbase, SpaceX also remains hard at work on launching data centers into space. Musk has already laid out the plans for a first-generation AI1 compute satellite with a 150kW peak compute payload, and submitted a proposal to build a 1-million-satellite Orbital Data Center System to the FCC. That work could accelerate after data center measures lost big in the poll in the recent U.S. midterm elections. In a post-election post on X, Musk ventured that “data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

#10381. Tag yourself as one of USPS’s new cryptid stamps

At the annual Mothman Festival in Point Pleasant, West Virginia, tens of thousands of visitors gather in their finest cosplay to commemorate the 1966 day that the “Mothman”—a 7-foot moth creature with bright red eyes—supposedly appeared from either the depths of hell or outer reaches of space to terrify onlookers. The festival is full of Mothman fans, for whom the legendary cryptid has morphed from a haunting specter to more of a lovable hero. Now, he’s getting his own official stamp. 

On November 9, the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) released an initial batch of stamp subjects for 2027. They run the gamut from traditional, subject-centric designs, like a stamp commemorating baseball’s Willie Mays, to designs aimed at a more artistic crowd, like a series of whimsical watercolor unicorns. 

The “Mythical Creatures” collection is a lineup of five American cryptids—the Mothman, Jackalope, Sasquatch, Squonk, and Champ—each designed by Antonio Alcalá, an art director at USPS, and illustrated by Nat Power, a tattoo artist. They’re sure to please folk historians, stamp collectors, and Reddit users alike. 

Meet Squonk, Jackalope, and Champ

Every year, USPS’s Citizen’s Stamp Advisory Committee (CSAC) restarts an intensive process of sifting through thousands of suggested topics from the public to land on the 20-25 new designs it recommends be produced. According to a 2024 USPS blog post, the final list has to be “uniquely American” and balance nods to topics like science, arts, history, and culture. The process leads to selections that traverse an array of genres, from Toni Morrison to Spongebob Squarepants.

The Mythical Creatures collection merges art history with American folklore. Its subjects are spooky, unknowable creatures that emerged in different regions of the U.S. The Jackalope is part of Wyoming legend after two taxidermist brothers created an antlered bunny in the 1930s; the Squonk is a Pennsylvania-based, pig-like cryptid whose main attribute of note is its constant weeping; and the Champ is a lake monster hailing from the Lake Champlain region in New York and Vermont.

The designs from Alcalá and Power take these myths and interpret them through the lens of American traditional tattoo aesthetics, rendering them in bold, dark lines with bright washes of color. The final products look less like the fare of an older letter-writing crowd, and more like the art you might find on the arm of a millennial who’s fallen down a few too many Reddit rabbit holes. 

In the 2024 blog post, Joe Kelley, the CSAC chair and a stamp collector, explained that the multigenerational appeal is often the point: “We want to highlight what’s great about America. The hope is to not only draw more people to the hobby of stamp collecting, but also encourage people to simply use stamps. With so much emphasis today on the popularity of all things ‘retro,’ why not be retro yourself and write a letter?”

#10378. Why Your AI Agent Can't Read the Web (and How to Build a Fetch Layer That Can)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

This is the least glamorous part of building with LLMs and it's where a lot of agent projects quietly fall over. The model is rarely the problem. The fetch is. In this article we'll look at why live web retrieval has become so unreliable for AI tools, what the numbers say about the shift, and how to build a small, well-behaved fetch layer in Python that fails loudly instead of feeding your model garbage.

A few years ago, a plain requests.get() worked on most of the public web. That's no longer true, and the reason is simple: there are now more bots than people.

According to the 2025 Imperva Bad Bot Report, automated traffic made up 51% of all web traffic in 2024. That's the first time in a decade it has passed human activity. Bad bots alone (scrapers, credential stuffers, scalpers) went from 32% to 37% of traffic in a single year.

Source: Imperva Bad Bot Report 2024 and 2025

From a site owner's point of view, your polite research agent and a credential-stuffing botnet look much the same at the network edge. Both are non-browser clients making fast requests from data-center IP ranges. So the defaults have tightened. In July 2025 Cloudflare began blocking known AI crawlers by default for new customers, and bot management products now look at TLS fingerprints, header order, IP reputation and JavaScript execution, not just the User-Agent string.

It helps to understand the publisher's side of the deal, because it explains why your agent is being treated with suspicion.

Cloudflare splits AI crawling into three purposes: training (collecting data to train models), search (building an index for AI search answers) and user action (fetching a page because a person just asked a question). Training dominates.

Training crawls take content and send nothing back. Cloudflare measures this with a crawl-to-referral ratio: how many pages a platform crawls for every visitor it sends to the site. In its crawl-to-click gap analysis, the ratios for some AI platforms ran into the tens of thousands, compared with single digits for traditional search.

If you ran a publication and saw those numbers, you'd block too. The catch is that blocking is usually done by user agent or IP range, so it hits user-action fetches as well. Those are the ones that happen when a person asks your agent to read a specific article, and Cloudflare's 2025 Year in Review found they grew more than 15x during the year. Your agent is caught in a fight it didn't start.

The mix of crawlers also shifts quickly, which makes static allow and block lists fragile on both sides:

And restrictions keep piling up. The Consent in Crisis study audited 14,000 web domains and found that a large and fast-growing share of the sources behind the C4 training corpus now restrict AI crawlers, either through robots.txt or their terms of service.

Source: Longpre et al., Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024)

So that's the environment your agent fetches in. Here's how to build for it.

Before writing any retry logic, put names on your failures. "The request failed" is useless to both you and the model. In practice almost every failed fetch falls into one of four buckets:

Bucket 2 is the dangerous one, because a block page often comes back with a 200 OK. If you don't check, the model will happily summarise "Checking your browser before accessing..." as if it were the article.

Here's a compact fetch layer in Python using httpx and the standard library's robots.txt parser. It's around 100 lines and covers the four buckets above.

Use a descriptive user agent with a contact URL. It costs you nothing and site operators are far more likely to allow a client they can identify and reach. Then check robots.txt (standardised as RFC 9309) before every new host.

The lru_cache means you fetch robots.txt once per origin rather than once per page. In a long-running service you'll want a cache with a TTL instead, since robots.txt files do change.

This is the core of the layer. Instead of returning raw HTML, return a result that says which bucket you landed in.

The marker list is deliberately simple. It won't catch every interstitial, but it catches the common ones, and a false "blocked" is much cheaper than a confident summary of a CAPTCHA page. Log every blocked result with its first few hundred characters so you can grow the list from real data.

Retries should depend on the bucket. Throttled and broken responses get exponential backoff with jitter. Blocked and not-allowed responses get no retries at all.

Note the cap on wait. A site sending Retry-After: 3600 is telling you to go away for an hour. An interactive agent should report that to the user rather than block a request thread for that long.

The cheapest fetch is the one you don't make. Agents often re-read the same documentation page several times in one session. Store the ETag and Last-Modified headers and send them back as If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since. A 304 Not Modified response costs the server almost nothing and lowers the odds of being rate limited.

Wire these into fetch() by passing headers=conditional_headers(url) to client.get(). On a 304, return the cached text. On a 200, call remember().

Finally, don't hide failures from the LLM. Give the tool output a structured shape so the model can reason about it:

(extract_main_text is whatever readability or boilerplate-removal step you already use. Libraries like trafilatura work well here.)

With this in place, the model's answer changes from a made-up summary to "I couldn't read that page because the site blocks automated access. Here's what I found from two other sources." That's a better product, and it builds trust with users.

Once you've done everything above, some legitimate user-action fetches will still fail. That's usually because the site blocks data-center IP ranges outright, not because of anything your agent did. Teams handle this in a few ways, roughly in order of preference:

The principle is the same in every case: the network path is a reliability decision, not a way around a site's wishes. Your robots.txt check and your honest user agent should stay in place whichever route the request takes.

Once your fetch layer returns structured results, observability is easy. Emit one event per fetch with the host, status bucket and latency, and watch these:

If you're prototyping agents with AI coding assistants, ask them to generate these metrics hooks from the start. They're easy to bolt on now and painful to add later. For a sense of how well current tools handle this kind of infrastructure code, Vibe Coder Journal publishes hands-on reviews and benchmarks of AI coding tools.

The web your agent reads in 2026 isn't the open, fetch-anything web many of us learned on. More than half the traffic is automated, publishers have good reasons to be wary of AI crawlers, and the defaults now lean toward blocking. You can't change that. You can make your agent a good citizen, though: one that identifies itself, respects the rules, backs off when asked, and tells the truth when it can't read something.

Most of the reliability gains come from the unglamorous parts: classifying failures, caching and passing honest errors to the model. Get those right and your agent will feel much more dependable, even on the days when half the web won't let it in.

It depends on the jurisdiction, the site's terms of service and what you do with the content. Respecting robots.txt and site terms is the baseline. For commercial products, get proper legal advice.

Many site owners expect it to, and RFC 9309 makes no exception for user-triggered fetches. The safest default is to obey it and tell the user when a page is disallowed.

Many bot-protection systems serve a challenge page with a 200 status. Check the body for challenge markers before passing it to the model, as in the looks_blocked() function above.

Only for pages that render their main content with JavaScript. Try a plain HTTP fetch first. Headless browsers are slower, cost more to run and are easier to fingerprint.
