#10377. A design legend’s oddball watches are back and cooler than ever

Tibor Kalman, the graphic designer, was known for confrontational stances; a “self-styled bad boy” of his profession, as The New York Times once described him. But Kalman—who was the editor in chief of Colors magazine and created album covers for The Talking Heads—produced plenty that was witty and warm before he died a quarter of a century ago, at age 49. Notably, this included a series of charming and celebrated wristwatches that his son, Alex, brought back into production. 

Analog watches may not seem like the most buzzy category in 21st-century retail, but these have, “for lack of a better word, a bit of a timeless design quality,” Alex Kalman says. In fact, design aficionados may recognize the three watches that have gone on sale this week through the website of M&Co Labs, Tibor’s design-product studio. They were originally part of a larger watch series tracing back to the late 1980s and early 1990s in which the elder Kalman treated the watch face as a space to subtly comment on time itself.

The watches became a flagship product for M&Co. In different ways, each gently challenges the functionality of a watch. One of them, dubbed “10-4-1,” eliminates all the hour numbers except for those three; it’s in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art. Another, “Onomatopoeia,” replaces some numbers with tiny pictograms: a cat for 9, an egg for 12. The third, “Askew” simply jumbles the numbers, apparently at random. On the back, all three are inscribed “Waste Not A Moment.” 

Today, the watches’ slightly impractical interfaces are arguably more subversive than when they were introduced. “It’s very funny that there’s all this effort for frictionless design, here is something so elemental as a watch face, but one that creates friction in trying to read the time on it,” Alex says. The urge to eliminate friction was present in Tibor’s era, but today it sometimes seems to be design’s primary function. “It’s come so much further than what he was initially reacting to,” Alex adds. And maybe that means it’s a perfect time for the watches to return.

Kalman became known for a distinct point of view, pushing his profession to face its social responsibilities, and tackling issues like race and AIDS in Colors. He also had a slew of client work, including design for musicians and the Times Square Redevelopment Corporation, under the auspices of M&Co. (The “M” stood for his wife and collaborator Maira Kalman, the artist, writer, and children’s book author.) In addition to the watches, the M&Co Labs spinoff produced a variety of clever objects, such as a paperweight shaped like crumpled paper, that were popular with the design-savvy set. 

After Tibor died in 1999, Alex says, Maira focused on her own work, making licensing deals with other firms to manage M&Co Labs’ product line. While the watches stayed in distribution for years, that supplier relationship eventually fizzled, and they fell out of production.

More recently, Maira and Alex (who is also a filmmaker and founder/curator of Mmuseumm, a mini-museum in a former freight elevator in lower Manhattan), decided to produce new batches of a few of the watches. It’s a tentative first step toward bringing back M&Co as a family business of sorts. 

“All the products, as the family likes to do, look at the conventions of things and play with them a little bit,” Alex says.

And that speaks to the potential appeal of the oddball, winky watches right now. When they were brand new, the watches were a means of “thinking of incredibly common vernacular everyday items that are part of our lives,” Alex says, “and how to play with them with that particular sensibility and share those ideas through everyday products, rather than just through design or editorial work.”

In a way, a time-keeping object’s role as material signifier of modernity is even more acute now that we track time on digital devices. A glance checking the hour may also bring news of a new follower, or a catastrophe. All the more reason, perhaps, to pause over that routine moment of noting where the clock stands. 

“The faces themselves, which is obviously really where the character is, have a lot of soul and wit and humanism,” Alex says. “And I think that’s a really nice thing to offer people in our increasingly slick technological landscape.”

It doesn’t hurt that for some the watches are both iconic and nostalgic, classic symbols of a distinct moment in product-design history with a certain pre-smartphone status. At least, this new iteration of M&Co Labs will find out if it’s true that there’s something meaningful in bringing these objects back. If it goes well, they’ll try physical retail: “Either on the corner of Canal Street or the MoMA Store,” Alex jokes.

#10376. AMD shares how it can retain 95% of server performance with just half the DRAM, sidestepping memory shortages with MEXT

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

MEXT offloads cold memory pages to flash storage and serves them up with a predictive AI model.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In June, AMD overtook the predictive memory engine known as MEXT, which claims to offer upwards of 99% of the performance of a system with full DRAM capacity while running with as little as 25% of the physical DIMMs. The technology offloads cold memory pages to flash storage and uses an AI model to serve pages before they’re needed, and AMD says it plans to extend the tech across a wide swath of its IT infrastructure next year.

The pitch behind MEXT seems too good to be true. According to AMD and MEXT founder Gary Smerdon, the technology can cut the physical DRAM required in a server by 20% to 75% depending on the application and performance target. That missing memory still registers as installed DRAM to the OS. Instead of DRAM, however, MEXT uses relatively inexpensive flash storage to offload cold pages, flying them back in as they’re needed with an AI model. In some of AMD’s internal workloads, such as Synopsys PrimeTime, the company says it’s able to achieve 95% of the performance of a full server while running at 50% DRAM capacity with MEXT.

AMD has deployed MEXT internally on 145 servers, which it says will expand to 2,000 servers next year. In addition, the company has announced a partnership with HPE to bring MEXT to customers. Currently, we’re in phase 1 of the rollout, with some EPYC Venice servers carrying a “MEXT Ready” badge and a dedicated NVMe drive or bay for the offload. Phase 2 brings MEXT licenses out to these servers, as well as the RAM View application. AMD hasn’t said when Phase 2 will begin.

The AI-driven DRAM pricing surge impacts more than just gaming PCs, with enterprises also feeling the brunt of price increases, even if they aren’t running AI workloads. If MEXT is able to achieve what AMD claims, it could be transformative given the current market. Because of that, it’s worth understanding what exactly MEXT is, as well as what AMD claims it can do.

Although MEXT is exciting in concept, it’s obvious that AMD is taking a conservative approach to the rollout. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, after all. The applications of MEXT are currently narrow, though AMD says it’s expanding the workloads it’s using MEXT on with promising early results.

The basic setup of MEXT is simple in concept: cold pages go to flash, AI brings those pages back as needed, and it’s as if the memory was never missing in the first place. The main problem should be obvious. Flash is orders of magnitude slower than DRAM, so streaming pages back into memory from flash as they’re needed isn’t feasible. MEXT’s trick is using an AI model to predict the pages you’ll need. And, as long as the model is able to stay ahead by at least the transfer latency from the SSD, it’s as if the physical DRAM was installed the whole time.

This isn’t a crazy concept considering how a transformer-based LLM, which MEXT uses, operates. If you’re unfamiliar with the inner workings, this open-source visualization breaks down the concept of a transformer AI model cleanly. The foundational concept is next token prediction, which underpins the design of modern LLMs. Given a set of tokens, the LLM determines which token (word, portion of a word, etc.) is most likely to come next. It makes a prediction. In the case of MEXT, it’s predicting what page is needed next, not what word comes next.

Memory offloading to flash isn’t a new concept, but MEXT founder Gary Smerdon says that AI is the critical difference in this technology. MEXT itself is deployed as a Linux kernel module that works with any Linux distro. It uses an “ensemble of AI models,” with the primary transformer-based LLM driving the technology. And critically, it doesn’t come pre-trained.

Instead, AMD says that MEXT trains in under a second when first deployed, operates on one EPYC core without a GPU, and continually trains as the workload progresses. This approach makes sense given the varied workloads that MEXT may apply to. The idea is that it would learn the access patterns of the application in order to drive that prediction engine.

MEXT isn’t perfect, but it doesn’t need to be perfect in every situation. For instance, the order of stored pages isn’t important. With text, an LLM needs to predict the correct text in the correct order, but with MEXT, the order doesn’t matter. As long as the page is in DRAM when it’s needed, that’s fine.

In order to understand the application of MEXT to different workloads, AMD has developed RAM View to go alongside the tech. It’s a memory utilization tool that shows which pages are hot and which have gone cold. As you can see from the example above, a system with 1.5 TB of memory shows near-full utilization across the full workload, but around half of the pages stored in memory haven’t been touched in five minutes or more at any given time.

AMD provided this generalized example and didn’t clarify what workload it was testing. That’s very important, as the utilization breakdown will look vastly different depending on the application(s) running on the server. Initially, AMD is applying MEXT to critical EDA applications it uses internally, such as Synopsys PrimeTime, but the company says it has focused on optimizing agentic AI, database, and media and entertainment workloads as well.

This is important not only because memory access patterns change between applications, but also because performance in those applications reacts differently when a system doesn’t have enough memory. The “memory wall,” as AMD calls it, should be a familiar concept regardless of whether you’ve ever touched a server. With MEXT, AMD says it’s trying to extend this memory wall, which may look different for different applications.

For instance, the company is confident that many workloads can reduce capacity by around 20% to 25%. As the reduction increases, however, the applications become more specialized, and the performance delta becomes greater.

AMD has shared some internal MEXT results, which look impressive, though as usual, it’s always smart to handle first-party benchmarks like this with skepticism. Starting with PrimeTime, where AMD has focused much of its attention on MEXT up to this point, it says servers running at 50% capacity retain 95% of the performance of a full server, and going down to as little as 25% capacity still maintains 80% of the application’s performance.

PrimeTime demands a lot of memory for large designs. There are some applications where performance is nearly identical, according to AMD. In a 3-node cluster running in Azure with 5th-gen EPYC CPUs, AMD says MEXT offers 99% of the performance of the full cluster while running at 50% DRAM capacity with the Spark SQL workload from the TPC-DS benchmark. SQL databases try to cache as much data as possible in memory to prevent I/O bottlenecks, creating a golden opportunity for tech like MEXT that wants to free cold pages.

Perhaps the most applicable workload at the current moment, however, is agentic AI, and AMD says MEXT has similar applications there. Across a five-agent concurrent geomean, AMD claims 99% of the performance of a full server with 50% memory capacity, and 85% of the performance with 25% capacity. With a “memory-hungry” agent, AMD claims 90% and 88% performance for 50% and 25% capacity, respectively.

The slide you can see above has footnote tags. However, AMD has not shared the footnotes with us yet, so we don’t have a view into how these tests were run. Naturally, we assume AMD has, at minimum, represented the performance of MEXT in the best light possible. We can’t do a full analysis without knowing how the tests were run, however.

What is interesting is AMD’s cautious approach to rolling out MEXT. It’s an EPYC-exclusive feature right now, though AMD left the door open for support on future products (consumer devices, such as Strix Halo) far down the road. It will be sold as a license, bundled with the RAM View software, but we don’t have a timeline on when that will happen. And, despite a partnership with HPE to push out “MEXT Ready” servers, we still don’t know when MEXT itself will be ready for deployment beyond AMD’s walls.

Given that conservative approach, there are likely pitfalls to MEXT that we’re not seeing yet, and it’s hard to imagine it will be broadly applicable to every server, at least at the 50% and 25% DRAM capacity levels that AMD showed off with its benchmarks.

However, even being able to trim 25% of a server’s DRAM capacity represents a massive cost savings in the current supply-constrained environment. If some workloads can push that to 50% capacity, that’s even better. Of course, we’ll need to see how MEXT holds up once it’s available broadly, but if AMD’s claims hold water, it could become a defining technology in data centers that can’t seem to get enough memory.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

#10374. Democrats won Congress. What might happen to Trump’s construction projects now?

The future of President Donald Trump’s construction and renovation projects in Washington, D.C., could soon come into question, after Democrats take control of Congress in January.

Trump has powered his pet projects through by sheer force of will since retaking office last year, setting a breakneck pace for ideas moving from blueprint to construction site. Disregarding legally mandated approval processes and protocols, his administration has knocked down buildings and torn up trees without permission.

Though legal challenges have, at times, slowed projects like the White House ballroom, arch monument, a D.C. golf course, and John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts renovations, they haven’t been effective.

The landscape is shifting, however. Once the the next Democrat-led Congress is in place, changes to the built environment will face oversight that Republicans didn’t previously provide. This is how it might shake out.

3 new roadblocks to Trump’s projects

First, Democrats will get two ex officio seats on the 12-person National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC)—the federal government’s D.C.-area planning agency—that are reserved for U.S. Senate and House of Representatives members. The president appoints some members of the commission, and there are others who are there because of their job titles.

Democrats will replace Senator Rand Paul and Representative James Comer, both Kentucky Republicans, with their own people. Those two new members of the commission could join with the District of Columbia’s four members, who have consistently voted against Trump’s building priorities, to block his projects from passing with a tied 6-6 vote.

Second, Democrats will have standing to sue in federal court on behalf of the Senate and House, using Senate and House counsel. Leveraging congressional subpoenas and investigations, lawmakers could learn more about private donations Trump used to fund the projects.

Third, and most important, Democrats will hold the purse strings in the appropriations process, which means they can restrict or defund executive branch activities. In addition to accepting private donations, Trump has also funded his construction with public, taxpayer funds. Under Democrats, that practice could soon come to an end.

What Democrats are saying

These potential roadblocks could be why Trump seems to be rushing to get construction work done before the next Congress is sworn in. The day after the midterm elections, Trump signed and raised a beam at the ballroom site. Meanwhile, the NCPC approved plans for his arch the following day, though a judge issued a temporary restraining order shortly after.

The restraining order lasts just 14 days, and Democratic lawmakers are gearing up to fight it long term.

Speaking about Trump’s arch, Representative Don Beyer, the Democrat whose northern Virginia district includes Arlington National Cemetery, said at a press conference Friday that he’s “never seen a project with such profound, widespread opposition from the very people who it will affect most.”

To fight the project, Beyer authored the Arlington National Cemetery Viewshed Protection Act, which would block the arch’s construction outright. Introduced in May, the bill hasn’t been brought to a vote under Republican House leadership. Under Democrats, that and similar legislation to defund or explicitly ban Trump projects could more easily make it to a vote.

Representative Jared Huffman, a California Democrat and ranking member on the House Natural Resources Committee, which oversees the Department of the Interior, said “the ground between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington belongs to the American people and the families who have buried loved ones there.” He warned officials who keep the project moving forward or firms that sign on to build the arch to “understand the legal risk they’re taking on.”

“If Trump wants a tribute to himself, he can build one at one of his glitzy resorts or private golf clubs,” Huffman said Friday in a statement. “Come January, a new Congress will demand answers from the people enabling this abuse of our public lands and our laws.”

For two years, Trump hasn’t faced pushback from Congress over his construction projects. That’s about to change.

#10371. Bending Spoons is buying up the internet. Can its business model last?

Bending Spoons has already acquired some of the internet’s most recognizable software brands. And it has identified more than 1,000 others it could potentially acquire.

The Milan-based company, whose portfolio includes Evernote, WeTransfer, Vimeo, AOL, and Eventbrite, disclosed the figure in its IPO prospectus. Together, those potential targets generated nearly $400 billion in estimated revenue in 2025.

Bending Spoons has hardly slowed down since its stock market debut in July. It has completed acquisitions of Airtable and Miro, and in October, Berkshire Hathaway invested another $330 million, bringing its ownership stake to 4%.

Its business model—buy an established product with paying customers, reorganize the company, reduce costs, improve the technology, and use the profits to pursue more acquisitions—is attracting attention across the software industry. And the results have generally been impressive.

But so have the job cuts. As AI makes software cheaper to develop and maintain, Bending Spoons may now be establishing a new model for an industry accustomed to prioritizing growth over profitability.

WHY BUYING OLD SOFTWARE MAKES FINANCIAL SENSE

Building a successful software business is expensive. A company could spend years developing a product, attracting customers, and trying to persuade them to pay for it with no guarantee it will succeed. Buying an established business, however, reduces some of that uncertainty.

“From an investor’s perspective, the fundamental advantage is that you’re buying proven behavior rather than financing the search for it,” says Vince Molinari, a financial services expert and founder and CEO of Fintech Media Group.

An established product already has customers, revenue, brand recognition, and a distribution network. For an acquirer, the opportunity often lies in improving how the business operates. Molinari places particular importance on customer retention. A company with loyal subscribers and inefficient operations may be more attractive than a fast-growing business whose customers regularly leave.

“Revenue tells you what customers paid yesterday. Retention helps tell you whether they’ll still be paying tomorrow,” he tells Fast Company.

Bending Spoons’ second-quarter results illustrate the appeal. Revenue rose 126% from a year earlier to $704 million, while operating income increased 139% to $240 million.

But acquisitions accounted for most of the revenue growth. Looking at its businesses without the extra revenue added by acquisitions, growth was just 3%. The figures show how heavily the company’s expansion still depends on buying businesses, rather than growing revenue from the ones it owns. “The next billion-dollar opportunity doesn’t necessarily start with the next big idea,” says Nadja Atwal, an international business adviser. “Sometimes it starts with recognizing that someone else’s old big idea still has plenty of life left in it.”

THE COST OF MAKING SOFTWARE MORE PROFITABLE

Bending Spoons is unusually willing to make sweeping changes after an acquisition. Its IPO filing disclosed that AOL, Eventbrite, and Vimeo collectively brought approximately 1,830 full-time-equivalent employees into the company. According to the filing, Bending Spoons planned to retain only a few hundred of those employees after restructuring the businesses.

The scale of such restructuring has attracted much criticism, but Vimeo offers an example of how Bending Spoons believes its approach can improve acquired products.

At Vimeo, Bending Spoons reported more than 30 product improvements during the second quarter, alongside a roughly 90% reduction in system-stability incidents compared with pre-acquisition levels. Uploads and searches also became at least 30% faster, according to the company.

These are encouraging results, although they are company-reported figures. Improvements in speed and reliability don’t necessarily tell us how customers feel about pricing, support, or the product’s direction.

Matteo Danieli, Bending Spoons’ cofounder and VP of product, told Fast Company⁠ last month that the company’s acquisition-driven growth gives its teams more freedom to concentrate on improving existing products. “We do not necessarily need to prove massive growth on products, and so we are actually free to focus on what’s useful for users,” he said.

Eliminating duplicated expenses, consolidating infrastructure, and improving how products are sold can make an acquired business substantially more profitable. But lower operating costs alone cannot establish whether a company is becoming healthier. Cutting too deeply can also mean losing experienced employees and the knowledge needed to maintain and improve a product.

“You can make almost any company look better for several quarters by cutting enough people and expenses. The real test is what happens three or five years later,” Molinari says.

Customers may judge the changes differently from investors. Faster software and new features can improve their experience, but higher prices, declining support, or unwanted product changes could weaken the loyalty that made these businesses attractive to acquire in the first place.

AI COULD CHANGE THE ECONOMICS EVEN FURTHER

Bending Spoons is betting that AI will help it accomplish more with smaller teams, and its own software-development figures suggest how quickly the technology is becoming part of its operations.

In its IPO prospectus, the company estimated that AI authored or coauthored more than 90% of software-code changes submitted for review by the end of March 2026, compared with less than 10% a year earlier.

That doesn’t mean AI independently builds or maintains its products. Engineers still have to review code, make decisions, and ensure software works reliably. But it demonstrates how extensively the company has incorporated AI into development.

Mohamed Mohamed, founder and CEO of applied AI company SmartBricks⁠ and a venture scout at a16z Speedrun, believes the implications could extend well beyond Bending Spoons’ engineering costs.

“AI is rapidly reducing the cost of developing, maintaining, and improving software,” he says. “That potentially makes acquiring established software businesses even more attractive because an acquirer can operate them with a fundamentally different cost structure.”

Marina Mogilko, an entrepreneur, investor, and creator who hosts the podcast Silicon Valley Girl, sees a parallel in the creator economy. She points to Electrify Video Partners’ majority investment in Veritasium, the popular science YouTube channel founded by Derek Muller. Electrify provides operational and commercial support while Muller retains an ownership interest and continues creating content.

“Centralizing operations, hiring, and monetization under one roof frees creative teams to focus on their craft, while giving the buyer decades of built-in brand trust and organic distribution that would cost a fortune to build from scratch today,” Mogilko says.

The comparison, while poignant, also has its limits. At Veritasium, for example, Muller remains central to the business, while Bending Spoons has often replaced much of the original workforce at companies it acquires. And that raises a question about how much institutional knowledge an acquirer can afford to lose while reorganizing a business.

CAN BENDING SPOONS KEEP ITS ADVANTAGE?

The reality is that the same AI tools that could make Bending Spoons’ acquisitions more profitable may also make the software it buys easier to compete against. As AI coding tools lower development costs, smaller teams can increasingly build products that once required far greater resources, putting pressure on established businesses to give customers compelling reasons to stay.

Cheaper software development could also change how investors value the businesses they acquire. “I believe we’re moving towards a world where the value of a software company is increasingly determined by the assets surrounding its technology rather than the technology itself,” SmartBricks⁠’ Mohamed says. That would give established software businesses an advantage only if their customers, distribution networks, and other assets remain difficult for competitors to replicate.

Bending Spoons has advantages that would be difficult for newcomers to match, including acquisition experience, access to financing, and an expanding technical operation. But acquisitions require capital, and the company ended June with approximately $4.09 billion in net debt. That increases the importance of generating lasting returns from the businesses it buys.

Mohamed believes those returns should be measured beyond immediate improvements in profitability. “Ultimately, the sustainability of this model depends on whether customer lifetime value improves, not simply whether EBITDA increases,” he says.

The list of more than 1,000 prospective acquisitions suggests that finding companies to buy is unlikely to be its immediate problem. But acquiring more businesses also means taking responsibility for the products and customer relationships that made them valuable. Mogilko thinks the biggest test comes after the deal closes.

“The real question—and the biggest risk to this model’s long-term sustainability—is how you maintain the soul of the company after replacing the original team and raising prices,” she says.

Bending Spoons has demonstrated how much financial value can be unlocked from established software businesses. Its growing portfolio suggests it has little intention of slowing down. But every acquisition brings customers whose loyalty was earned long before Bending Spoons arrived. The company’s future may depend as much on giving them reasons to stay as on finding the next business to buy.

#10370. Hunter is killing Google Home, Alexa controls for its smart ceiling fans

Hunter, a major brand for ceiling fans in the US, is pulling the plug on its Google Home and Amazon Alexa bridge for controlling “HunterSMART” models in just a few weeks.

Effective January 1, 2027, Hunter will pull support for the cloud-reliant “HunterSMART” connection used for Google Home and Amazon Alexa controls. Hunter’s app and the included remote will continue to work, but connections to smart home ecosystems will not.

Beginning January 1, 2027, the legacy cloud-to-cloud connections used for app linking between the HunterSMART™ mobile apps and Google Home and/or Amazon Alexa will no longer be supported.

After this date, Google home and Alexa functionality that relies on this legacy cloud connection will no longer work for HunterSMART fans, including voice commands, scenes, and automations.

This bridge is going away in favor of a Matter connection, with Hunter having been upgrading select models to be Matter-compatible over the past year. But this is only available to “eligible” models, not everyone who was already using Hunter’s existing bridge. A list of compatible models is available on Hunter’s website, with firmware updates rolling out via the HunterSMART app.

Some models, such as the one I reviewed a few years ago, require updated hardware. Besides that, the one I have can’t even be re-connected to Wi-Fi to check for an update as Hunter’s Android app consistently crashes during the setup process.

Once the fan has been updated, it won’t be available via the existing link and will instead require re-pairing via your smart home app of choice, whether that’s Google Home or another.

…Hunter is transitioning eligible HunterSMART™ products to Matter, an industry standard designed to support broader smart-home compatibility.

If your fan is eligible for Matter-compatibility, you will be able to continue using all smart functionality within the Google Home and/or Alexa ecosystems after completing the applicable Matter migration & setup.

Once your HunterSMART fan is Matter-enabled, connecting your fan to Google and Alexa will work differently than it does today. Instead of linking your HunterSMART account to Google Home or Alexa, you will need to setup your Matter-enabled fan directly into these compatible ecosystems using the Matter setup available via the Google Home and/or Alexa apps. Matter-enabled devices do not use the legacy cloud linking service for smart controls that is being discontinued.

How can I migrate my HunterSMART fan to Matter?

Depending on your fan model and hardware configuration, a firmware update or updated hardware components may be required for Matter compatibility. Available Matter upgrade options and instructions will vary by product. You can visit our HunterSMART™ Matter resource page for the latest information about Matter compatibility, available upgrade options, and next steps.

#10367. CLEAR is giving members 5 free airport guest passes for the holidays. Here’s how to get them

Holiday travel can be stressful enough without worrying about getting everyone in your group through airport security. This year, CLEAR is introducing a new perk that could make things a little easier for members, their friends, and family.

Starting today, CLEAR members can share up to five free Holiday Guest Passes with friends and family who aren’t already members, giving them access to the company’s expedited airport security service for 14 days.

And there’s an especially useful detail: You don’t have to be traveling with someone to send them a pass. The passes are part of a broader holiday travel push from CLEAR that includes a redesigned app, new gift cards, personalized airport assistance, and the company’s biggest membership discount of the year.

How to get CLEAR’s free holiday guest passes

For the holidays, CLEAR is making guest passes available directly through its mobile app, allowing members to share them with a single tap.

“If you’re a CLEAR member, you’ll be able to open your CLEAR app, and you’ll see them, and you’ll have up to five to send to family and friends who are not members,” Campbell Millum, CLEAR’s vice president of communications, told Fast Company.

That means members can send a pass to someone traveling across the country, even if they aren’t flying together.

“If you know that your friend is traveling, if you know your mom is traveling, or a friend or family member, you can go ahead and send those, and then they can have the experience of CLEAR at what we know is the most stressful time of the year to travel,” Millum said.

Recipients will need to stop at CLEAR’s airport pods to enroll before using the service. Once enrolled, they’ll have access to CLEAR for 14 days, potentially covering both their outbound and return flights.

CLEAR’s new app helps travelers get from home to gate

Alongside the guest passes, CLEAR is introducing an upgraded app designed to help travelers navigate more than just airport security. The app now features Planning Mode and Travel Mode, which automatically adapt to different stages of a trip.

Planning Mode helps travelers prepare before leaving home, including booking a ride to the airport and calculating when to leave based on traffic conditions and their preferred airport arrival time.

Once travelers arrive at the airport, Travel Mode takes over, helping them locate CLEAR+ lanes, estimate the walk to their departure gate, and access services such as CLEAR Concierge.

The app also supports Live Activities, allowing travelers to receive real-time updates on their phone’s lock screen.

“We want to help members win the day of travel from home to gate and back again,” Millum said. “We hear all the time, and I know for myself, that travel isn’t just about the moment you get to the airport. It starts long before when you’re at home, when you’re planning, and then all the way through to when you get to your gate.”

Millum said the company wants to take some of the guesswork out of travel by bringing information and services into one place.

“We know that between your flight, the traffic, and the walk to your gate, we want the app to do the math so that you don’t have to,” he said, noting that the app uses real-time information to help travelers plan their airport arrival, rather than relying solely on historical estimates.

“We want to make sure that whenever holiday travel is already stressful because of all the unknowns, you’re [not left] asking, ‘When do I leave? Where’s my gate? How far is my gate?’” she said.

The company is also introducing gift cards, allowing customers to purchase its services for friends, family members, employees, or clients.

The busiest holiday travel days, according to CLEAR

The announcement comes as CLEAR prepares for what it expects to be a particularly busy holiday travel season.

Based on historical travel patterns, the company predicts Sunday, November 29, will be the busiest day of the season for its members, with security lines expected to be especially crowded between 5 and 7 a.m. and remain busy until 6 p.m. local time.

For Christmas, CLEAR expects Friday, December 18, to be the busiest departure day, with additional crowds anticipated on December 22 and 23. The return rush is expected to peak Sunday, December 27, with crowds beginning to ease around 5 p.m.

The predictions are based on CLEAR’s own travel patterns rather than nationwide airport passenger totals, so actual airport conditions may vary.

When developing a website, developers often rely on CSS classes to style buttons, forms, navigation elements, and other interface components. This approach works well, but some situations require styles to depend on an element's HTML attributes rather than additional class names.

CSS attribute selectors provide a practical solution. They allow developers to target elements based on whether an attribute exists, what value it contains, or whether its value matches a particular pattern. Used carefully, they can simplify styling and make reusable components easier to maintain.

An attribute selector targets an HTML element using square brackets. For example, a developer can select every input field that has a required attribute:

This rule applies to inputs with the required attribute, regardless of their input type.

Developers can also target a specific attribute value:

This is useful when different input types need different visual treatments without introducing additional classes into the HTML.

Forms are a practical place to apply attribute selectors because HTML already provides attributes that describe how individual fields behave.

Consider a registration form containing email, password, and telephone fields. Each input can be styled according to its purpose:

The CSS can target these fields independently:

This approach keeps the markup descriptive while allowing the stylesheet to respond to the attributes already present in the document.

One important distinction is that required indicates a validation requirement, while :invalid represents an input's current validity state. These should not be treated as interchangeable.

CSS provides several matching operators that help developers target more specific attribute values.

These operators can be useful when working with links, downloadable files, language attributes, and reusable components.

For example, a website might want to distinguish PDF downloads from ordinary navigation links:

This adds a small visual indicator to links whose URLs end in .pdf.

Attribute selectors can also help identify links with different destinations or behaviors.

For example, external links that use HTTPS can receive a subtle visual indicator:

However, matching an HTTPS URL does not necessarily prove that a link points to an external website. Internal links can also use HTTPS, so developers should consider the actual navigation requirements before applying special styling.

For more examples of selector combinations and matching rules, SitePoint's guide to CSS Attribute Selectors provides a useful reference.

Although attribute selectors are flexible, they should not replace every class-based styling decision.

A selector such as [class*="button"] can match unintended elements if their class names happen to contain the same text. Similarly, broad attribute rules may affect components that were not originally intended to receive those styles.

For predictable results, use exact attribute matching whenever possible and prefer descriptive classes for major component styling.

Developers should also remember that CSS selectors only control presentation. They do not replace JavaScript validation, server-side security checks, or proper HTML semantics.

The MDN documentation on attribute selectors provides further details about selector syntax, matching behavior, and supported operators.

Before adding attribute selectors to a large stylesheet, inspect the affected elements using browser developer tools.

Check whether the selector matches the intended elements.

Test fields with different attribute values.

Verify disabled, required, and invalid form states.

Check navigation links and downloadable files.

Test the layout on mobile and desktop screens.

Review whether existing component styles are being unintentionally overridden.

This process helps identify unexpected matches before they affect the production interface.

CSS attribute selectors give developers another way to create flexible and maintainable interfaces without adding unnecessary classes to every HTML element.

They are particularly useful for form styling, link identification, and components that already contain meaningful HTML attributes. By choosing precise selectors, understanding matching operators, and testing changes before deployment, developers can use this feature to write cleaner CSS while keeping their markup descriptive and organized.

#10364. A new guideline doesn’t change care

Early in my career as a neonatologist, group B streptococcus (GBS) was one of the infections we feared most. Babies who appeared healthy could become critically ill within hours or days, leaving physicians to tell parents that their newborn was suddenly fighting a life-threatening infection.

Eventually, evidence gave us a way to prevent many of those infections. Researchers found that screening pregnant women for GBS, and treating those who tested positive with antibiotics during labor could dramatically reduce transmission to newborns. Professional societies issued recommendations. But practice did not change overnight.

It took years of clearer guidelines, physician education, and standardized workflows before universal GBS screening became embedded into routine prenatal care. I spent much of my career developing and implementing evidence-based guidelines across neonatal and population health programs. That experience taught me something healthcare needs to pay more attention to today: A guideline can tell clinicians what good care looks like, but on its own it cannot make that care happen.

That matters as medicine advances faster than our healthcare system’s ability to incorporate those advances into everyday practice.

THE GAP BETWEEN EVIDENCE AND ACTION

Clinical research asks whether a diagnostic or treatment works. Implementation science asks what happens next: If we know something works, what will it take to make sure patients receive it?

GBS screening offers useful lessons. Early recommendations gave clinicians multiple approaches. Over time, guidance became more decisive and universal screening became the standard. But guidelines were only part of what changed.

Healthcare built a reliable system around them. The recommendation became a workflow. There was clear timing set for screening, a standard test, a straightforward result, and an established intervention. Responsibility for each step needed to be clear until the process became routine.

That is the lesson we should carry forward as we consider some of the most promising advances in medicine today.

GENOMIC MEDICINE IS AN IMPLEMENTATION CHALLENGE

While innovation is here, there are implementation challenges. Genomic sequencing is a good example. Evidence supporting exome and genome sequencing has expanded significantly, particularly for children with suspected genetic conditions. Clinical guidelines increasingly recognize its role in helping patients reach a diagnosis earlier.

Guidelines, though, are a leading indicator of change, not the endpoint.

Putting genomic testing into practice is more complex. For a clinician, the diagnostic journey starts with connecting subtle clinical clues to a potential hereditary etiology. What follows is a demanding progression of matching symptoms to the right test, guiding the family through pre-test choices, and deciphering complex findings into a tailored care plan.

Once a diagnosis is confirmed, it reshapes the trajectory on various levels by modifying treatments. It establishes surveillance protocols and potentially identifies at-risk relatives. Every transition, though, creates another opportunity for adoption to break down.

Meanwhile, operational friction looms over the entire path. Insurance roadblocks and limited access to specialized genetics colleagues, along with cumbersome documentation routines often overshadow the clinical merits. Even the strongest guidelines will fail to shift behavior when the everyday reality makes acting on them nearly impossible.

CLOSE THE GAP BETWEEN GUIDELINES AND PRACTICE

If we want medical innovation to reach patients, we need to design for implementation from the beginning. Can the right patient be identified easily? Does the clinician know when testing is appropriate? Is ordering simple? Is coverage predictable? Can the result be understood and acted upon? Is it clear who owns the next step?

And critically, can the process work not only at leading academic medical centers with deep specialty resources, but in the places where most patients actually receive care?

Today, we have tools that can accelerate this transition. Clinical decision support can help identify patients who may benefit from testing. Digital ordering can reduce administrative burden. AI can help clinicians navigate complex information. Telehealth can extend access to genetics expertise.

But the goal should be to remove the friction between what medicine knows and what clinicians can realistically do.

WE BUILD THE STANDARD OF CARE

Healthcare often talks about achieving standard of care as though it happens when enough evidence accumulates or a professional society updates its recommendations. My experience has taught me to think about it differently.

A true standard of care exists when the right care happens reliably across physicians, health systems, geographies, and patient populations without requiring extraordinary effort from the clinician or patient. Guidelines are essential, but they have to be translated into coverage and workflows. They need to be included in education and clinician confidence, as well as provide access.

The history of GBS screening shows us that evidence can transform medicine, but only when we build the systems that allow clinicians to act on it. Genomic medicine is a more complex implementation challenge, but the lesson is the same.

We have spent decades getting better at discovering what works in medicine. Now we need to become just as good at making it work in the real world.

Linda Genen, MD, MPH, is chief medical officer at GeneDx.

#10363. Googlebook apps built by Googlers add macOS-like status bar shortcuts, keyboard commands

Googlebooks are a bit starved of desktop-class features at launch, but one of Google’s pitches around this platform is how apps can be built for it, and the company’s own employees are showing off what that looks like with some clever apps that just so happen to add features that feel a lot like they’re replicating macOS staples.

In a Reddit thread, three Googlebook apps built by Googlers through Antigravity are shown off, and they’re pretty cool, regardless of how you might feel about the platform itself.

“BentoBox” is a utility that gives you control over the status bar on Googlebook, enabling you to fill the status bar with shortcuts, mini-apps, and more. It’s full of glancable information such as weather conditions, battery charging speeds, and more, but also includes useful tools such as being able to access a clipboard history, set a timer, and more. The app requires permissions including accessibility overlays, but it works like a charm.

I had no idea the status bar on Googlebook could even be used like this, and it really makes that space a lot more useful. Of course, you have to draw a comparison here to macOS, which also uses this space for app shortcuts and tools, though BentoBox offers a different type of customization.

BentoBox is available for download via Google Play for free.

The other Mac-like app here is “Booklight,” a launcher that’s basically Apple’s Spotlight, just for Googlebook. It has a transparent design and lets you search “apps, settings, and the web.”

Technically, Googlebook already can do this in its built-in search bar (in the app drawer), but Booklight has more customization and functionality, including being able to write out shorthand commands all in one sentence with the app then completing the command in the appropriate apps, as well as having a clearer UI for experiences such as typing in quick math equations. It’s also good at finding symbols (so you don’t have to remember the U+ codes that carried over from ChromeOS). Not one I found myself wanting to use, but the potential is there.

Both BentoBox and Booklight were developed by Alexander Kuscher, VP over Laptops & Tablets at Google.

The other app highlighted in Google’s thread was Wayfinder, a file manager app described as a “desktop-grade file manager.” The big bonus here is network file access for NAS boxes and other uses, but the app also just has a more advanced UX compared to Googlebook’s built-in Files app.

Googlebook’s app gap is a real problem at launch, but these apps do show there’s a lot of potential in the platform, it’s just a matter of getting developers on board – which itself will require Google and its partners to actually sell some of these laptops… classic chicken-and-egg situation.

The Linux Kernel is probably one of the best ecosystems to observe regarding the impact of AI in programming. The critical importance of its code and its maintainers' quality standards mean that patches, including but not only AI slop, go through rigorous review and are often discarded. Still, the amount of AI-produced code is often far higher than what the human reviewers can deal with. Lorenzo Stoakes, a lead Linux reviewer for memory management, has elected to step down from some of his former duties for exactly that reason.

Stoakes announced his decision today in a thread on the Linux kernel mailing list (LKML). He'll be leaving the core, reclaim, Rust, THP (Huge Pages), and miscellaneous sections of the kernel memory management section, while staying on for his remaining duties, including KVM. The partial departure appears amicable, and the developer doesn't appear to be angry or bitter. He says that his decision was due to the mounting pressure on his inbox, that he'll wrap up the patch series he's currently working on, and he'll occasionally pitch in regardless.

However, the underlying cause is also clear: "Of course the AI wave has been horrible, and is getting significantly worse. At first it was once in a while that I'd see slop. Then it was at least once a week. Then every few days. Nowadays it's pretty much half of what I see, if not more."

This is a sentiment echoed by many programmers in the open-source community, and the latest in a running series of AI-provoked project departures, submission rules adjustments, and strategic shifts. AI-assisted programming has arguably been both a boon and a curse for open-source software. The project's open nature means that anyone can find a bug and report it or fix it, or add functionality — all of which are good things.

However, that also means that literally anyone can contribute, and in a world ridden with low-effort AI slop and untold amounts of AI agents, that's... suboptimal. Open-source projects are arguably the hardest-hit because they very rarely have the adequate manpower or funds to keep the code up to date, much less deal with the output of a million robotic monkeys on a million digital typewriters.

Linus Torvalds, creator and headmaster of Linux, has taken a pro-AI stance, supported not only by the speed of additional contributions, but also the fact that bots often don't make mistakes that even seasoned developers do. This topic has been the subject of a lot of LKML discussion, and the current stance is that AI-assisted code commits don't need to be marked as such.

The problem, then, has arguably become one of filtering: it's easy enough to be accepting of AI contributions when your day isn't spent waddling through mud to find the one gold nugget, which is what Stoakes was seemingly weary of.

Even as recently as a month ago, he said that "what kills the project is having 1,000 slop submissions that 2 or 3 people have to do something with."

#10360. The best AI lab in business is not for sale—you already own it

The last time every client wanted to talk about the same thing at the same time, it was Y2K. It is happening again with AI, but with a key difference. This time, the money is outpacing the understanding.

From the internet to cloud to mobile, each technology wave follows the same pattern. Companies rush in and treat adoption as a what question, while it should be a who question.

We lead firms with different specialties. BDO’s is assurance, tax, and advisory; Gagen MacDonald’s specialty is people-centered change. Working together on BDO’s AI transformation confirmed what we both see with organizations: Technology creates the possibility of transformation, but people determine whether it succeeds.

WHY THE RETURNS AREN’T SHOWING UP

As boards set their 2027 budgets, one question will follow AI spending into nearly every conversation: Why isn’t it showing up in our results? Intelligence platform AI4SP found that for the first half of 2026, 76% of enterprise AI initiatives struggled to show return on investment, while in 2025, Gartner projected that more than 40% of agentic AI projects would be canceled by the end of 2027.

The reflex is to write a bigger check for a more capable platform. But buying more of what companies have struggled to turn into value cannot be the fix.

We believe most firms treat AI as a technology purchase. We treat it as a people transformation. Hand the best tools in the world to people who have no reason to care, and you have bought expensive software nobody uses.

But the response should not be a top-down mandate nor a pure grassroots initiative. At BDO, we call it guided grassroots: Leadership sets the direction, and the people closest to the work build the solutions. We are equipping and encouraging each of BDO’s 14,000-plus team members to find where AI belongs in their work, within parameters and guardrails.

LISTEN BEFORE YOU SPEND

Before we spend big on anything new at BDO, we listen. Our technology partner ran an anonymous diagnostic that nearly 3,500 colleagues answered in April and May. The results showed that 87% were already using AI, and more than 11,000 ideas came back for how our professionals could use AI to improve their work and processes.

Interestingly, almost nobody asked for an additional or different platform. They asked for help from AI with the many small things that rob people of time that could be spent on client relationships, developing their teams, and deep work. This proved the innovation engine already existed. It now needed structure, support, and governance to scale.

MAKE IT VISIBLE, THEN SCALE IT

BDO’s AI champions, embedded across the firm, help colleagues find useful applications, experiment within guardrails, and share what works, so ideas spread sideways. A firm-wide dashboard makes the work visible. It details which agents are in use, who built them, and who else relies on them.

At BDO, the rule is simple. Our people build it, we measure business impact, and we scale what works. Before our first formal training session, more than 600 team members had already built over 1,200 working agents. Two weeks after training an initial group of champions, the number of agents built had increased by roughly 80%, and the number of builders had grown by more than 50%.

To contextualize those numbers, consider when BDO’s brand language changes, which often happens twice a year. Updating nearly 2,000 design files used to take 20 people close to a month. Emma, one of our creative professionals, used AI to shape an automation that updates the designs in about a day. It only took one person. Encouragingly, the other 19 employees are still on that team. The month they used to lose to rework now goes back into the creative work they were hired to do.

Finding meaningful ways to help people effectively use AI is the first challenge. Keeping active what people build is another. Our technology partner’s research finds that without the internal capacity to continually maintain and improve agents, more than 60% of users stop engaging with them within three months. An agent creates value as people continue to use it, which means organizations need the internal capacity to sustain and improve what they build.

HOW BOARDS SHOULD LOOK AT IT

We do not recommend uncontrolled adoption. Leaders decide which tools people use, what information those tools can reach, and how to verify outputs. BDO’s first practice-wide agent is for quality checks. It flags what a reviewer should look at and preserves human judgment and decision-making authority.

As boards ask where the returns are, they should consider whether they have built an organization capable of discovering what AI is good for and then scaling what they find.

Outside providers will remain essential for models, infrastructure, and technical expertise. But they equip the lab. They are not the lab. The best AI lab in business? You already own it.

Maril Gagen MacDonald is the founder and CEO of Gagen MacDonald. Matthew Becker is the chief executive officer of BDO USA.

#10358. Fitbit Sense & Versa losing 3rd-party watch faces this month, existing downloads remain

Google announced today that Fitbit Sense and Versa smartwatches will soon lose the ability to “install or update third-party apps and clocks.”

This change to the Fitbit App Gallery applies to the Versa, Versa 2, Versa 3, Versa 4, Sense, and Sense 2.

Existing “third-party apps or clock faces installed on your Fitbit device” will remain available, but you can no longer download new ones (or update them) starting November 28. As such, “if you choose to delete an app or clock face, or factory reset your device, you will no longer be able to re-install it.”

Instead, the Fitbit App Gallery will “exclusively feature apps and clock faces created by Fitbit and Google.”

The November 28 deadline also applies to third-party developers. Google will “no longer support uploading new apps and clock faces or updating existing ones.”

Google winding down Fitbit OS for smartwatches is not particularly surprising as the company has been all-in on Wear OS and the Pixel Watch. That said, the Sense 2 and Versa 4 should probably no longer be on sale.

#10357. Jensen Huang resigns: Nvidia shares tumble even further after scandal-ridden CEO replaced with interim boss

Update: Thursday, 9:15 a.m. ET:

Jensen Huang has resigned as president and CEO of Nvidia, the company’s board of directors announced on Thursday.

The move caps a dramatic week for one of the most influential titans of tech, who had become embroiled in scandals surrounding two extramarital affairs, one with an alleged spy and another with a subordinate.

Huang’s resignation is effective immediately.

Colette Kress, who is currently Nvidia’s EVP and CFO, has agreed to serve as Interim CEO until a permanent replacement can be found, Nvidia said. The company’s lack of a cohesive succession plan has caused concern among analysts and investors alike.

Premarket shares of Nvidia Corp. (Nasdaq: NVDA) fell even further on Thursday morning following the news of Huang’s departure.

As of this writing, the stock is down almost 13% in premarket trading. That’s in addition to an 11.33.% decline over the last five trading sessions.

This story is developing…

Original story appears below:

Shares of Nvidia Corporation (Nasdaq: NVDA) are once again sinking in premarket trading this morning after reports yesterday that the company’s board has convened to discuss whether to oust its embattled cofounder and CEO, Jensen Huang.

As of this writing, NVDA shares are down more than 7% in premarket trading, mainly due to uncertainty over Huang’s fate.

But several Wall Street analysts worry that Nvidia’s lack of a known succession plan could weigh on the stock’s price for a long time. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happened?

This week started out bad for Nvidia, and yesterday things got worse.

On Sunday, CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials believe could be a Chinese spy. That raised severe national security concerns and led to a steep sell-off in NVDA stock.

However, at the time, Nvidia’s board released a statement saying it still had “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”

In other words: it was a scandal, but the board backed its CEO (and said it had no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised).

But things got worse yesterday.

That’s when The Wall Street Journal revealed that Nvidia’s board was meeting to determine whether to oust Huang. What changed? News broke of an alleged second affair that Huang had had, this time with a subordinate who works at Nvidia.

At this time, Huang’s fate remains unknown. But it’s precisely that uncertainty—and what comes next if he is ousted—that has Wall Street fearing for NVDA stock.

Nvidia has no publicly known succession plan

One of the greatest periods of anxiety and uncertainty for employees and investors is when a company changes leadership. 

If the old leader was good, can the new one measure up? Will the new leader change tack? Will the bottom line be impacted? Will the corporate environment change? What about employee morale and productivity?

Leadership changes often bring these kinds of questions, even in ideal situations, when a CEO change has been telegraphed long in advance (as was done with Apple’s CEO transition earlier this year).

But when a CEO change happens on short notice, especially when a scandal is driving it—and the company has no known succession plans in place—that really freaks investors out.

And that’s exactly why Nvidia stock is falling so much this morning.

The company has no known succession plans for who will take over when Huang leaves the CEO role. That only adds to the uncertainty now. It’s not only: Will he be fired? It’s: Who can successfully run one of the world’s most valuable and economically important companies if Huang is ousted?

Who can replace Huang as Nvidia CEO?

It should be noted that Nvidia may have a secret succession plan in place that the company has never publicly disclosed. But if they did, the board would likely have acknowledged the plan—or at least its existence —given the uncertainty of Huang’s fate.

Regardless of whether a plan is in place, if Huang were to be ousted, Nvidia has two options for replacing him: find a new CEO from within Nvidia, or look outside. 

It’s impossible to predict which external person the company would select as the new CEO, but someone with a deep understanding of AI or chip design would be likely. 

If Nvidia looks inside, there are some obvious candidates, based on their positions at the company:

  • Colette Kress: the company’s chief financial officer.
  • Ian Buck: VP of Hyperscale and High-Performance Computing
  • Michael Kagan: the company’s chief technology officer

CNBC reports that Citi analysts Atif Malik and Papa Sylla think Kress is a likely interim option while Nvidia searches for a permanent successor.

Morningstar says that if Nvidia recruits internally, Buck “strikes us as a logical successor to Jensen Huang” and “is well known to outside investors.”

But the fact of the matter is, for now, no one knows who would replace Huang.

Nvidia stock turns negative for the year

All this uncertainty is weighing on NVDA stock. As of this writing, Nvidia shares are down nearly 7.5% in premarket trading, bringing their five-day loss to over 13%—a staggering amount for a company that many see as the backbone of the AI economy.

Many investors fear worse times for NVDA ahead because of the scandal. The company is already being sued by shareholders, and a series of congressional investigations is likely.

Then the ever-present question remains: Who leads Nvidia if its visionary CEO is forced out?

“Right now, Nvidia doesn’t have [a Tim Cook to Steve Jobs-type] person in place, so it’s going to be a choice of keeping Jensen and being faced with . . . all kinds of interrogations, or they’re going to have to move on from him,” Questar Capital Partners’ Richard Reyle noted to CNBC, “and that’s just going to make the stock uninvestable.”

Uninvestable or not, the company’s share price has fallen more than 33% since its all-time high above $239 in early October, when Nvidia was valued at more than $5.7 trillion—the most valuable public company in history. 

Today, post-Huang scandal, the company’s valuation is down to less than $4.2 trillion.

(Disclosure: Morningstar is owned by Joe Mansueto, owner of Fast Company parent Mansueto Ventures.)

Listeria monocytogenes outbreaks continue to spark food recalls across the country.

This time it’s Family Farmstead Dairy, which has recalled all of its cheddar cheese products due to a potential listeria contamination, according to a notice posted by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

“This action is being taken as part of our ongoing commitment to continuous improvement and product excellence,” Family Farmstead Dairy stated in the recall. “The company remains committed to producing safe, high-quality dairy products and maintaining the trust of the communities it serves.”

The FDA announcement comes less than a month after the Worcester, New York, company recalled some of its raw cheddar products due to potential E. Coli O26:H11 and O45:H2 contamination. 

Here’s what you need to know about the latest Family Farmstead Dairy recall. 

What products are affected?

The recall is for two Family Farmstead brand cheddar cheeses. Here’s all the information you need to identify them:

Raw Mild Cheddar, 8oz, plastic wrapped

  • All lot codes dated October 16, 2027 or sooner

Raw Sharp Cheddar, 8oz, plastic wrapped

  • All lot codes dated October 16, 2027 or sooner

Where and when was the product sold?

Right now, we don’t know exactly when or in which stores the recalled cheddar cheeses were sold. All we know is which states they were distributed in:

  • Connecticut
  • Delaware
  • Massachusetts 
  • New Hampshire
  • New Jersey
  • New York
  • Pennsylvania
  • Rhode Island
  • Tennessee
  • Vermont
  • Virginia 
  • West Virginia

What should I do if I have this product? 

You can either return the impacted cheese to your point of purchase or contact Family Farmstead Dairy for assistance. The company is available at customerservice@familyfarmsteaddairy.com or (607) 397-4044 from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. ET, Monday to Friday. 

What listeria symptoms should I look out for? 

Listeria is an organism that can cause sickness in people of all ages. Healthy individuals exposed to listeria will likely experience short-term symptoms including:

  • Abdominal pain
  • Diarrhea 
  • High fever
  • Severe headache
  • Stiffness

A listeria infection during pregnancy can lead to miscarriages or stillbirths.

Young people, elderly individuals, and anyone with a weakened immune system are at risk of more serious or even fatal results.

Intel and AMD NPU support is planned, but founder says neither will be used for language models.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A team led by Cyanogen co-founder Kirt McMaster has unveiled Kora, a new Linux desktop OS with integrated AI models and agents that can split workloads across CPU, GPU, and NPU resources, as well as other machines on the same local network. We reached out to the firm for more info.

Kora, the first product from Kora Systems Inc., previously Playtron, carries the tagline “The Operating System for Intelligence” and has its own Cortex “hybrid inference engine” technology, which is not open source and is optimized for local models. The OS, built “from the kernel to the shell,” runs local models by default and cloud models when needed, and is expected to arrive on PCs in 2027.

The desktop follows the AI-focused motif with “neural workspaces” and a “neural file system,” which refer to sandboxed workspaces and files indexed by semantic meaning. Kora has three operating modes: “Work," "Create," and "Play." That last base is covered by GameFrame, which descends from Playtron’s GameOS. Humain OS, which Kora is developing with Saudi AI company Humain, is the enterprise variant of this OS.

Currently, the only NPU named in the release material is the Hexagon NPU found in the Snapdragon X2 Elite, which Qualcomm pegs at 80 TOPS. On the X2 Elite, Cortex can schedule AI workloads across the CPU, GPU, and NPU, as well as other systems on the local network, which could be a novel capability if it works beyond the Qualcomm hardware.

McMaster told Tom’s Hardware that the Snapdragon X2 Elite NPU runs Google's Gemma 4 26B model at 25 tokens per second for decode. Intel and AMD NPU support is in the works, but according to the developer, neither NPU will be used for LLMs, as GPUs are “just better for LLM workloads on x64.”

Each NPU vendor has its own software stack, or runtime, and prefers that models are compiled in its own format: Qualcomm with QAIRT/QNN, Intel with OpenVINO, and AMD with Ryzen AI software. The press kit doesn't identify support for any Intel or AMD chip, NPU runtime, model format, quantization, or speed figures for those platforms.

Our earlier Windows testing showed the same kind of divide: Snapdragon reached its NPU through the QNN provider under ONNX Runtime, while Intel’s work ran through IPEX, its extension for PyTorch, on the GPU because it was faster than the NPU.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

When asked about cross-vendor support, McMaster reiterated that “only Hexagon on Snapdragon X2 Elite is supported today.” Intel NPU support is planned, with “conversations underway,” though McMaster later clarified that neither Intel’s nor AMD’s NPU will be used for LLMs. On AMD’s Ryzen AI chips, Kora will likely use the NPU for embedding and speech-recognition models through ONNX.As for what drives the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU, McMaster said Kora uses the “llama.cpp Hexagon backend” and “the upstream FastRPC driver.” That suggests the operating system reaches the NPU through the open-source llama.cpp project, not Qualcomm’s own QAIRT/QNN runtime, by way of the FastRPC driver in the mainline kernel.

Language models; KORA cites Gemma 4 26B at 25 tokens per second

Likely embedding and speech-recognition models; not language models

When asked about model formats, McMaster said, “we predominantly support GGUF,” llama.cpp’s model file format, and that Lemma, the inference engine inside Cortex, “can split model layers across processors as needed.” Lemma is built on llama.cpp, whisper.cpp, stable-diffusion.cpp, and ONNX. McMaster says that which runtime is used depends on the model's requirements, and more runtimes will be added down the line.

For today, llama.cpp has a Hexagon backend for Snapdragon and an OpenVINO backend for Intel CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, although the latter is still marked “In Progress,” and no AMD NPU backend, which would explain why AMD goes through ONNX. AMD NPUs can run LLMs on Linux through the separate Lemonade 10.0 stack with FastFlowLM, as reported by Phoronix in March, though that isn’t the route Kora has chosen.

Beyond NPU stacks, those hoping to run Kora will need to be mindful of their system's available memory. The Gemma 4 26B model Kora uses, which Google lists as Gemma 4 26B A4B, needs about 14.4GB of memory to load its weights at 4-bit (Q4_0) quantization, by Google’s estimate, before any context window, while third-party listings put the download for the Q4_K_M file Kora uses at about 16–17GB. The model only activates about 4 billion of its 26 billion parameters per token but still needs to be fully loaded into memory.

McMaster said that with the model, the X2 Elite reaches “25 TPS decode throughput and 550 TPS prefill throughput,” or tokens per second, running “entirely on the Hexagon NPU with 32K context.” A dense model, rather than a mixture-of-experts, would be far slower. Not given are the RAM configuration or the specific X2 Elite chip.

On memory, McMaster said that “we recommend 64GB because it gives you access to better models,” but that is not a firm requirement. The company projects that “about 70 percent of the model calls it manages will run locally in 2027.”

Kora says its enterprise-focused Humain OS is due first and will be “commercially available in 2027,” on OEM PCs using the Snapdragon X2 Elite. Kora will follow "later in 2027.”

McMaster says that “Kora will be posted on our site and downloadable for anyone to install.” Included will be a list of recommended configurations, “but it should be installable on most modern PCs.” Exact pricing and the overall business model will be shared closer to the date of availability.Edit: 11/11/2026 9:06am PT: Added further follow-up details provided by the maker.
